application-layer.title: Application layer: HTTP, DNS, e-mail, FTP

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: At which OSI layer is the protocol data unit called a frame?
options: Physical layer
Transport layer
Data link layer
Network layer
questions.explanation: The data link layer wraps a network-layer packet with a header (MAC addresses) and a trailer (FCS), producing a frame. The network layer's unit is a packet, and the physical layer handles raw bits, so neither is called a frame.
questions.concept: PDUs: bits (L1), frames (L2), packets (L3), segments/datagrams (L4).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In classful addressing, to which class does 172.16.5.4 belong?
options: Class C
Class A
Class D
Class B
questions.explanation: The first octet 172 lies in 128-191, which means the leading bits are 10, so it is Class B. Class C begins at 192 (leading bits 110).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which transport and port does DNS normally use for ordinary queries?
options: TCP port 443 only
TCP port 25
UDP port 67
UDP port 53 (TCP 53 for zone transfers and large responses)
questions.explanation: Most DNS queries are small, so they use UDP 53 for speed; TCP 53 is used for zone transfers and responses that do not fit. UDP 67 belongs to the DHCP/BOOTP server.
questions.concept: DNS: UDP 53 normally, TCP 53 for zone transfers.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In socket(AF_INET, type, 0), which type selects TCP?
options: SOCK_RAW
SOCK_STREAM
PF_UNIX
SOCK_DGRAM
questions.explanation: SOCK_STREAM gives a reliable byte stream (TCP) and SOCK_DGRAM gives datagrams (UDP). PF_UNIX is an address family for local IPC, not a socket type.
questions.concept: SOCK_STREAM = TCP; SOCK_DGRAM = UDP.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the TTL field and the ICMP Time Exceeded message?
options: To stop packets circulating forever in routing loops and tell the source when one is discarded
To limit how long a TCP connection may stay open
To encrypt the packet after a set number of hops
To measure link bandwidth
questions.explanation: Each router decrements TTL; at zero the packet is dropped and the source is told with Time Exceeded. TTL counts hops, not connection lifetime, so the second option confuses layers.
questions.concept: TTL bounds a packet's lifetime in hops.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does a MAC flooding attack do to a switch?
options: It changes the switch's own MAC address
It encrypts frames so the switch cannot read them
It overloads the switch's routing table with fake IP routes
It fills the CAM table with bogus MAC addresses so the switch floods frames out of every port like a hub
questions.explanation: When the CAM table is full, unknown destinations are flooded, so an attacker on any port can sniff traffic. Switches forward on MAC tables, not IP routing tables.
questions.concept: CAM overflow -> fail-open flooding -> sniffing.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does DNSSEC defend against cache poisoning?
options: It encrypts all DNS queries end to end
It switches DNS from UDP to TCP
Authoritative servers sign records and resolvers verify the signatures, rejecting forged data
It hides the transaction ID from attackers
questions.explanation: DNSSEC provides origin authentication and integrity of DNS data with public-key signatures. It does not encrypt queries, which is the job of DNS over TLS or HTTPS.
questions.concept: DNSSEC = signed DNS data, not encrypted DNS.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which Snort rule action takes effect only when Snort runs inline as an IPS?
options: log
drop
alert
pass
questions.explanation: drop (and block, reject) discard packets, which is only possible when Snort sits in the traffic path. alert and log work in passive IDS mode as well.
questions.concept: IDS: alert/log/pass; inline IPS adds drop/block/reject.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does a one-time pad need to achieve perfect secrecy?
options: A truly random key at least as long as the message, never reused
A key of 128 bits used for every message
A secret algorithm known only to the two parties
A key derived from the user's password
questions.explanation: Shannon showed perfect secrecy needs |K| >= |M| and fresh keys; reuse leaks m1 XOR m2. A fixed 128-bit key for every message may be computationally secure but is not perfect secrecy.
questions.concept: OTP: random, as long as the message, used once.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: On which hard problem does Diffie-Hellman key agreement rely?
options: Finding hash collisions
The discrete logarithm problem
Integer factorisation
The knapsack problem
questions.explanation: Given g, p and g^a mod p, recovering a should be infeasible for large p. Factorisation is RSA's hard problem.
questions.concept: DH = discrete log; RSA = factoring.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why do two hosts with two-way IPsec traffic need two security associations (SAs)?
options: SAs expire after one packet
Each host can store only one SA
One SA is for AH and the other must be for IKE
An SA is simplex (one-way), so each direction needs its own
questions.explanation: Each SA protects traffic in one direction with its own keys and SPI. IKE has its own separate SA, but that is not why data traffic needs a pair.
questions.concept: SA = one-way; bidirectional traffic needs two.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does steganography differ from encryption?
options: Steganography hides the existence of a message inside a carrier; encryption makes a visible message unreadable
Steganography always uses stronger keys
Encryption hides data inside images
They are the same technique
questions.explanation: A stego image looks normal, while ciphertext is obviously ciphertext. Encryption does not hide data in images; that description belongs to steganography.
questions.concept: Stego conceals presence; encryption conceals content.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A packet travels host S -> R1 -> R2 -> R3 -> server. Compare the frame R2 sends to R3 with the frame R1 sent to R2. What has changed?
options: Nothing changes, because frames are forwarded unmodified end to end
The TCP source and destination ports are rewritten at each hop
Only the source and destination MAC addresses; the IP addresses and ports are unchanged
The source IP is rewritten to R2's address and the destination IP to R3's
questions.explanation: Each router strips the incoming frame and builds a new one with its own MAC as source and the next hop's MAC as destination, while leaving the IP header addresses intact. Rewriting IP addresses per hop would make end-to-end routing impossible (NAT is a special case, not normal forwarding).
questions.concept: Per hop: MAC addresses change; end-to-end IP addresses and ports do not.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the network address of the host 10.45.77.200/20?
questions.explanation: A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0. In the third octet, 77 AND 240 = 64, so the network is 10.45.64.0. 10.45.77.0 wrongly assumes a /24 boundary; 10.45.80.0 is the next block, not the one containing .77.
questions.concept: Network ID = IP AND mask; the interesting octet decides the answer.
questions.source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 19

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A page has one HTML file and 5 images. Using non-persistent HTTP/1.0 with serial requests and ignoring transmission time, how many RTTs elapse before everything arrives?
options: 10 RTTs
6 RTTs
12 RTTs
7 RTTs
questions.explanation: Each object needs its own TCP connection (1 RTT) plus the request/response (1 RTT): 6 objects x 2 RTT = 12. 7 RTTs is the persistent-connection figure (1 handshake + 6 requests).
questions.concept: Non-persistent: ~2 RTT per object; persistent: 1 RTT per object after setup.
questions.source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 27

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A TCP segment has sequence number 34,500 and carries 1,460 bytes. If it arrives correctly, what acknowledgement number does the receiver send?
questions.explanation: ACK = sequence number of the first byte + data length = 34,500 + 1,460 = 35,960 (the next byte expected). 35,959 is the last byte received, not the next one expected.
questions.concept: ACK number = last byte received + 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Host S sends a packet with TTL = 3 towards R through routers R1, R2, R3 and R4. Where is it discarded, and who is told?
options: At R4, which sends Time Exceeded to S
At R3, which sends ICMP Time Exceeded to S
At R, which sends Destination Unreachable to S
At R2, which sends Time Exceeded to R1
questions.explanation: R1 decrements 3 to 2, R2 to 1, and R3 to 0; R3 is not the destination, so it drops the packet and reports to the source. ICMP errors go to the original source, never to the previous router.
questions.concept: The router that decrements TTL to 0 discards and reports to the source.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An attacker captures a valid authentication token and sends it again an hour later to gain access. Which attack is this?
options: Masquerade without capture
Traffic analysis
Modification of message
Replay
questions.explanation: A replay re-sends a captured valid data unit unchanged to produce an unauthorised effect. Modification would alter the contents; here the token is reused exactly as captured.
questions.concept: Replay = capture and retransmit a valid unit.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A DHCP pool has 120 free addresses. An attacker sends 400 DISCOVER messages per minute with unique MACs. Roughly how long until the pool is exhausted?
options: 18 minutes
3.3 minutes
18 seconds
0.3 seconds
questions.explanation: Time = free addresses / rate = 120/400 = 0.3 min = 18 s. Reading 0.3 as seconds (or 18 as minutes) is the unit slip the notes flag in a slide.
questions.concept: Exhaustion time = free addresses / request rate; watch the units.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An off-path attacker triggers a lookup of a domain it controls and sees transaction ID 3,150. The resolver uses sequential IDs. Which ID should the attacker put in forged replies to the resolver's next query?
options: Any random value, since IDs are not checked
questions.explanation: Sequential IDs make the next query's ID predictable (ID + 1), so the attacker races the genuine reply with 3,151. Reusing 3,150 would match the old query, which has already been answered.
questions.concept: Sequential transaction IDs let off-path attackers predict the next ID.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does the tcpdump filter 'tcp[13] & 0x12 == 0x02' capture?
options: Only initial SYN segments (SYN set, ACK clear)
Only RST segments
Any segment with SYN or ACK set
SYN-ACK segments only
questions.explanation: Byte 13 holds the flags; masking with 0x12 keeps SYN (0x02) and ACK (0x10), and requiring 0x02 means SYN on, ACK off. SYN-ACK would give 0x12 after masking, so it is excluded.
questions.concept: Mask the flags byte, then compare.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Encrypt the letter 'm' with the additive cipher, key k = 17 (a = 0).
options: D
R
V
E
questions.explanation: 'm' = 12; (12 + 17) mod 26 = 3 = 'D'. 'V' comes from subtracting the key, which is decryption.
questions.concept: C = (P + k) mod 26.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A 4-stage LFSR has state (z0, z1, z2, z3) = (1, 0, 0, 1). Each tick it outputs z0, shifts left, and sets the new z3 = z0 XOR z1. What are the first 8 output bits?
questions.explanation: Ticks: output 1, new bit 1^0=1 -> (0,0,1,1); output 0, new 0^0=0 -> (0,1,1,0); and so on, giving 10011010. '10010001' uses taps z0 and z3 instead of z0 and z1; '10011001' simply repeats the seed.
questions.concept: Track the full state each tick: output, shift, insert feedback.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Diffie-Hellman with p = 29, g = 2. Alice picks a = 5, Bob picks b = 11. What shared key do they compute?
questions.explanation: A = 2^5 mod 29 = 3, B = 2^11 mod 29 = 18; K = B^a mod p = 18^5 mod 29 = 15 (and A^b gives the same). 3 and 18 are the public half-keys, not the shared key.
questions.concept: K = B^a mod p = A^b mod p = g^(ab) mod p.
questions.source: Scenario type: Kaufman, Perlman & Speciner, Network Security, ch. 6

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An AH header carries a 96-bit ICV after its 12 fixed bytes. What value goes in the AH Payload Length field?
questions.explanation: Total AH length = 12 + 12 = 24 bytes = 6 32-bit words; the field holds words minus 2 = 4. Writing 6 forgets the minus-2 rule.
questions.concept: AH Payload Length = (AH length in 32-bit words) - 2.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A file named invoice.jpg begins with bytes 4D 5A 90 00. What should the examiner conclude?
options: It is a ZIP archive
It is a PNG image renamed to .jpg
It is a corrupted JPEG
It is a Windows executable disguised with an image extension
questions.explanation: 4D 5A ('MZ') is the DOS/PE executable signature; a JPEG would start FF D8 FF. A corrupted JPEG would still normally keep its SOI marker.
questions.concept: Extensions can lie; magic numbers do not.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An attack path has three hops with trust (success) values 0.9, 0.7 and 0.5. What is the path's combined trust score?
questions.explanation: Series hops multiply: 0.9 x 0.7 x 0.5 = 0.315. 2.1 adds the values, which would exceed 1 and cannot be a probability.
questions.concept: Series: T = T1 x T2 x ... x Tk.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A public web portal suffers both HTTP floods and SQL injection. Budget allows one new control this quarter. Which choice is best justified?
options: Switch port security, because it limits how many hosts can connect
Doubling uplink bandwidth, because floods then cannot fill the link
uRPF on the edge router, because it removes all malicious traffic
A web application firewall with rate limiting, because both attacks live at Layer 7 and need payload-aware inspection
questions.explanation: Both threats are application-layer: floods use valid HTTP requests and SQLi hides in request bodies, so a WAF with request-rate controls addresses both. uRPF only removes some spoofed-source traffic; HTTP floods normally come from real, unspoofed bot addresses over completed TCP connections.
questions.concept: Choose controls at the layer where the attack operates.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which control set best protects users of a café Wi-Fi network against Ettercap-style ARP man-in-the-middle attacks?
options: Client isolation and DAI with DHCP snooping on the network, plus mandatory HTTPS with HSTS for services
A longer DHCP lease time and a larger address pool
Static ARP entries on every customer laptop, entered by staff
SYN cookies on the access point
questions.explanation: Isolation and DAI stop poisoning at the network, and HTTPS/HSTS keep data safe even if a MitM succeeds. Static ARP on transient customer laptops is unmanageable and leaves the access point's own table open.
questions.concept: Layer the defences: prevent poisoning, and encrypt in case prevention fails.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: For a new secure messaging protocol, which stream-cipher choice is best justified?
options: A 64-bit LFSR, because it is fast in hardware
RC4 with a 256-bit key, since longer keys remove its biases
ChaCha20 (with Poly1305 authentication), because RC4's biases have led to its prohibition in TLS
RC4-drop[768] without authentication, since dropped bytes make it unbreakable
questions.explanation: ChaCha20-Poly1305 is a modern, well-analysed authenticated design. Longer RC4 keys do not remove its keystream biases, and dropping initial bytes leaves long-term biases and gives no integrity.
questions.concept: Choose current, authenticated primitives over patched legacy ones.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which OSI layer is responsible for process-to-process delivery using port numbers?
options: Data link layer
Transport layer
Network layer
Session layer
questions.explanation: Ports identify the process on a host, and the transport layer (TCP/UDP) uses them for multiplexing and demultiplexing. The network layer only gets a packet from host to host; it has no notion of which application should receive it.
questions.concept: Network layer = host-to-host; transport layer = process-to-process.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the default subnet mask of a Class C network?
questions.explanation: Class C uses three octets for the network ID and one for hosts, so the default mask is /24. /26 is a subnetted Class C mask, not the default.
questions.concept: Default masks: A /8, B /16, C /24.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why is FTP described as an out-of-band protocol?
options: It needs an e-mail server to deliver the files
It sends commands over UDP and files over TCP
It uses a separate control connection (port 21) and data connection (port 20 or dynamic)
It carries commands and file data on one TCP connection
questions.explanation: FTP keeps commands and replies on a persistent control channel and opens data connections per transfer. HTTP, by contrast, is in-band: commands and content share one connection.
questions.concept: FTP: control 21 (persistent), data 20 (per transfer).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why does server code call htons(PORT) before bind()?
options: To convert a host name into an IP address
To choose a free ephemeral port
To convert the 16-bit port from host byte order to network (big-endian) byte order
To encrypt the port number
questions.explanation: Protocol headers use big-endian order, but many CPUs are little-endian, so htons converts the value. Converting names to addresses is a resolver function, not htons.
questions.concept: htons = host-to-network short (16-bit).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the main advance of DHCP over BOOTP?
options: DHCP assigns MAC addresses to clients
DHCP can lease addresses dynamically from a pool for a set time, as well as use static bindings
DHCP no longer needs relay agents
DHCP uses TCP instead of UDP
questions.explanation: BOOTP relies on a static MAC-to-IP table; DHCP adds a pool with lease times and renewal. DHCP still uses UDP 67/68 and still needs relay agents across routers.
questions.concept: DHCP = static + dynamic (leased) allocation.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which property of ARP makes ARP spoofing possible?
options: ARP runs over TCP, which can be hijacked
ARP is stateless and unauthenticated, so hosts accept unsolicited replies and overwrite cache entries
ARP replies are always broadcast
ARP is encrypted with a weak key
questions.explanation: Hosts cache any ARP reply, even one they never asked for, with no check of who sent it. ARP is not encrypted at all, and it is carried directly in Ethernet frames rather than over TCP.
questions.concept: No authentication in ARP -> forged IP-to-MAC bindings.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In a DNS amplification attack, whose address appears as the source of the attacker's small queries?
options: The root server's
The open resolver's
The victim's
The attacker's own
questions.explanation: Spoofing the victim's address makes the reflectors send their large responses to the victim. Using the attacker's own address would send the flood back to the attacker.
questions.concept: Reflection/amplification: spoof the victim as the source.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does httprobe do?
options: Scans all 65,535 TCP ports on each host
Crawls every link on a site
Tests web servers for known CVEs
Reads domains from standard input and prints the http:// and https:// URLs that respond
questions.explanation: httprobe checks whether hosts answer HTTP/HTTPS (ports 80/443 by default, plus custom ones). It does not scan non-HTTP ports or test vulnerabilities.
questions.concept: httprobe = live web-service discovery.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts stream and block ciphers?
options: A stream cipher uses two keys; a block cipher uses one
Block ciphers never need padding
RC4 is a block cipher and AES is a stream cipher
A stream cipher encrypts one bit or byte at a time with a keystream; a block cipher encrypts fixed-size blocks, padding the last one
questions.explanation: RC4 and ChaCha20 are stream ciphers; DES (64-bit blocks) and AES (128-bit blocks) are block ciphers that pad the final block. The last option swaps the two families.
questions.concept: Stream = symbol by symbol; block = fixed chunks plus padding.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: On which hard problem does RSA rely?
options: Inverting a hash function
Factoring the modulus n = p x q into its primes
Solving linear equations over GF(2)
Computing discrete logarithms mod p
questions.explanation: Knowing p and q gives phi(n) and hence d; without them d is out of reach for large n. Linear equations over GF(2) are how LFSRs are broken.
questions.concept: RSA security = hardness of factoring n.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which three values identify a security association?
options: Source port, destination port and protocol
Source IP, TTL and SPI
SPI, destination IP address and security protocol (AH or ESP)
Encryption key, MAC key and lifetime
questions.explanation: The receiver uses the SPI in the header, plus destination and protocol, to look up the SA in its SAD. Keys and lifetime are stored in the SA entry; they do not identify it.
questions.concept: SA identifier: (SPI, destination, protocol).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which of these is system metadata rather than application metadata?
options: The author name inside a Word document
EXIF GPS coordinates in a photo
Revision history embedded in a PDF
A file's modified, accessed and created (MAC) timestamps
questions.explanation: The file system maintains timestamps, permissions and ownership; application metadata lives inside the file, such as EXIF or document properties. GPS coordinates are written by the camera into the file itself.
questions.concept: System metadata: file system; application metadata: inside the file.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Router R2 on a path is compromised. The application payload is protected with TLS. What can the attacker on R2 read from transiting packets?
options: Nothing at all, because TLS also encrypts the IP and TCP headers
Only MAC addresses, because routers never examine IP headers
Source/destination IP addresses and TCP ports, plus link-layer MACs, but not the plaintext message
The plaintext message, because routers decrypt traffic at Layer 3
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts the application data above TCP, so headers below it (IP addresses, ports) stay readable to any hop. Claiming TLS hides IP and TCP headers is the common mistake; those headers must stay in clear for routing and delivery.
questions.concept: Encryption protects only what is above the layer that applies it.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the directed broadcast address of 172.20.130.17/18?
questions.explanation: A /18 block in the third octet has size 64: blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192. 130 falls in 128-191, so the broadcast is 172.20.191.255. 172.20.255.255 would be the broadcast of the whole /16.
questions.concept: Broadcast = network ID with all host bits set to 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: The same page (1 HTML + 5 images) is fetched with persistent HTTP/1.1 without pipelining. How many RTTs, ignoring transmission time?
options: 6 RTTs
12 RTTs
7 RTTs
2 RTTs
questions.explanation: One RTT sets up the TCP connection, then each of the 6 objects needs one request/response RTT on the same connection: 1 + 6 = 7. 12 RTTs would mean opening a new connection per object.
questions.concept: Persistent connections pay the handshake once per session.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An IPv4 packet has total length 1,200 bytes, IP header 20 bytes and a TCP header with options of 32 bytes. The TCP sequence number is 7,000. What is the acknowledgement number for this segment?
questions.explanation: Data = 1,200 - 20 - 32 = 1148 bytes, so ACK = 7,000 + 1148 = 8148. 8,160 assumes a 20-byte TCP header and ignores the 12 bytes of options.
questions.concept: Payload = IP total length - IP header - TCP header.
questions.source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 23

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Traceroute sends a probe with TTL = 4 and receives a Time Exceeded message. What does that reveal?
options: That the destination is four hops away and reachable
The identity (address) of the fourth router on the path
That the fourth router is congested
That the destination port is closed
questions.explanation: Each TTL value makes the router at that hop expire the probe and reply, revealing its address. Reaching the destination would instead produce a reply from the host (e.g. Port Unreachable or Echo Reply), not Time Exceeded.
questions.concept: Traceroute maps hops by incrementing TTL: 1, 2, 3, ...

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A manager sends 'ADD user G, ADD user H'. An attacker alters it in transit to 'ADD user I' and the server applies it. Which property is violated, and which attack is it?
options: Availability; denial of service
Confidentiality; release of message contents
Integrity; modification of message
Confidentiality; traffic analysis
questions.explanation: The content was changed in transit and accepted as genuine, so integrity is broken by an active modification. Nothing was disclosed, so confidentiality is not the violated property.
questions.concept: Modification attacks violate integrity.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A server's SYN backlog holds 4,096 half-open connections. A flood arrives at 20,000 SYNs per second. How fast does the backlog fill?
options: About 0.205 seconds
About 30 seconds, the SYN-RECEIVED timeout
About 4.88 seconds
About 12.3 seconds
questions.explanation: t = B / R = 4096/20000 = 0.2048 s. The timeout only controls when entries expire; it does not set how fast the queue fills.
questions.concept: Fill time = capacity / arrival rate.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A resolver randomises both the 16-bit transaction ID and the 16-bit UDP source port. How many combinations must a blind attacker cover?
questions.explanation: Independent 16-bit values multiply: 2^16 x 2^16 = 2^32. Adding them (2^17) is the classic mistake; combinations multiply, not add.
questions.concept: Port randomisation multiplies the guessing space.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An analyst uses 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' to count connection attempts during a suspected flood. What is wrong?
options: It matches nothing because tcpflags is not a valid name
It counts UDP packets too
It also matches SYN-ACK replies, so it overcounts; use tcp[13] & 0x12 == 0x02
It matches only RST packets
questions.explanation: Any segment with the SYN bit set passes, including the server's SYN-ACKs. tcpflags is a valid tcpdump keyword, so the filter does work, just too broadly.
questions.concept: SYN != 0 also catches SYN-ACK.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Decrypt ciphertext letter 'C' from the additive cipher with key k = 9.
options: u
l
t
h
questions.explanation: 'C' = 2; (2 - 9) mod 26 = 19 = 't'. A negative result must be wrapped by adding 26, not dropped or made positive by sign change.
questions.concept: P = (C - k) mod 26; add 26 to negative values.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: For the same LFSR (new z3 = z0 XOR z1, feedback polynomial x^4 + x + 1), what is the period starting from any non-zero seed?
questions.explanation: x^4 + x + 1 is primitive, so the register cycles through all 15 non-zero states before repeating. 16 would include the all-zero state, which never leaves itself.
questions.concept: Primitive polynomial -> maximal period 2^L - 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A relay sees g = 3, p = 19 and Client 1's half-key A = 7. Brute-forcing exponents from 1 upwards, which private value a does it find?
questions.explanation: Powers of 3 mod 19 run 3, 9, 8, 5, 15, 7, ..., so 3^6 mod 19 = 7 and a = 6. a = 4 gives 5, which is the value used in the corrected lab example.
questions.concept: Tiny primes make the discrete log trivial by brute force.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In ESP tunnel mode protecting an IPv4 packet, what is the Next Header value in the ESP trailer? And in transport mode carrying TCP?
options: 50 in both modes
17 in tunnel mode; 6 in transport mode
6 in tunnel mode; 4 in transport mode
4 in tunnel mode; 6 in transport mode
questions.explanation: Next Header names what is inside: an entire IPv4 packet (4) in tunnel mode, or a TCP segment (6) in transport mode. 50 is ESP's own protocol number, which appears in the outer IP header.
questions.concept: Next Header: 4 = IPv4 inside; 6 = TCP inside.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A file named report.docx starts with 50 4B 03 04. Signature analysis should flag it as ...
options: a mismatch: it is really a PDF
a mismatch: it is really a ZIP archive, not a document
an executable disguised as a document
consistent: Office Open XML documents are ZIP containers
questions.explanation: DOCX, XLSX and PPTX are ZIP packages, so 'PK\x03\x04' is expected; a check of the internal [Content_Types].xml would confirm. Flagging it as a mismatch is a classic false positive.
questions.concept: Know container formats before flagging mismatches.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Two independent attack paths reach the same node with trust values 0.6 and 0.5. What is the combined (parallel) trust?
questions.explanation: Parallel paths combine as an OR: 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.6 x 0.5 = 0.80. 0.30 multiplies, which is the series rule.
questions.concept: Parallel: T = TA + TB - TA x TB.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: You are designing defence in depth for a branch LAN with guest Wi-Fi and a public web app. Which layer-to-control mapping is the most complete and correctly placed?
options: L2: DAI, DHCP snooping, port security; L3: ACLs with uRPF; L4: SYN cookies and rate limits; L7: WAF and strict TLS settings
L2: SYN cookies; L3: DAI; L4: WAF; L7: uRPF
L1: TLS 1.3; L2: uRPF; L3: HttpOnly cookies; L7: shielded cabling
L2: WAF; L3: SYN cookies; L4: DHCP snooping; L7: port security
questions.explanation: Each control sits where its attack class lives: switches guard ARP/DHCP/MAC tables, routers filter addresses, hosts protect TCP state, and the web tier inspects HTTP. The other mappings put controls at layers where they cannot see the traffic they claim to filter, such as a WAF at Layer 2.
questions.concept: Defence in depth = the right control at every layer, not one control everywhere.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: You run the edge router for an organisation that owns 203.0.113.0/24. Which ingress/egress filtering design correctly limits spoofing?
options: Drop inbound packets whose destination is in 203.0.113.0/24
Drop inbound packets whose source is in 203.0.113.0/24, and drop outbound packets whose source is NOT in 203.0.113.0/24
Drop outbound packets whose source IS in 203.0.113.0/24
Allow everything but log packets with SYN set
questions.explanation: Outside traffic should never claim your own prefix as its source, and your own hosts should only send with your prefix. Dropping inbound packets addressed to your own network would block all legitimate traffic.
questions.concept: Ingress: no inside sources from outside; egress: only inside sources leave.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: You must fix a chat client that reuses one RC4 key for all messages. Which redesign is sound?
options: Prepend the message number to the plaintext but keep the same key
Derive a fresh per-message key from the shared secret and a unique counter with a KDF, and use an authenticated cipher such as ChaCha20-Poly1305
Encrypt each message twice with the same RC4 key
Discard the first 10 keystream bytes of the same key for each message
questions.explanation: Unique keys (or nonces) per message prevent keystream reuse, and authentication adds integrity. Encrypting twice with the same keystream cancels out; discarding the same 10 bytes every time still repeats the rest of the keystream.
questions.concept: Unique key or nonce per message, plus authentication.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: When forwarding a packet, up to which OSI layer does an ordinary router process it?
options: Transport layer (Layer 4)
Network layer (Layer 3)
Application layer (Layer 7)
Data link layer (Layer 2) only
questions.explanation: A router reads the destination IP address and consults its routing table, which is Layer 3 work; it then re-frames the packet for the next hop. It does not need TCP/UDP ports to forward, so Layer 4 is not part of ordinary forwarding.
questions.concept: Routers are Layer 3 devices; switches Layer 2; hubs and repeaters Layer 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A host sends a packet to 255.255.255.255. Which statement is correct?
options: It is a directed broadcast forwarded to every network on the Internet
It is a multicast address for routing protocols
It is a limited broadcast delivered to all hosts on the local network and never forwarded by routers
It is the network address of the local subnet
questions.explanation: All-ones is the limited broadcast; routers contain it within the local segment to avoid broadcast storms. A directed broadcast keeps a real network ID with an all-ones host part, such as 20.255.255.255.
questions.concept: Limited broadcast stays local; directed broadcast targets a remote network.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why was MIME introduced for e-mail?
options: SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII text, so binary and non-Latin content must be encoded (e.g. Base64)
SMTP could not carry messages longer than 512 bytes
To replace POP3 for mailbox retrieval
To encrypt e-mail end to end
questions.explanation: MIME encodes images, audio, documents and other non-ASCII data into 7-bit text and labels it with headers such as Content-Type. It does not encrypt anything; S/MIME and PGP add security.
questions.concept: MIME = encoding bridge from binary to 7-bit ASCII and back.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does a CRC differ from a cryptographic hash?
options: A CRC prevents an attacker from altering data
A CRC can correct any single-bit error
A CRC needs a secret key shared by sender and receiver
A CRC detects accidental bit errors but gives no protection against deliberate tampering
questions.explanation: CRCs are linear and keyless, so an attacker who modifies data can simply recompute a matching CRC. They detect noise but do not correct it; correcting errors needs other codes.
questions.concept: CRC = error detection for noise, not integrity against attackers.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What are the three objectives of the CIA triad?
options: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
Control, integrity, accountability
Confidentiality, identity, authorisation
Cryptography, inspection, auditing
questions.explanation: The core triad is confidentiality, integrity and availability; authentication and accountability extend it. Accountability is an extension, not one of the three core objectives.
questions.concept: CIA + authenticity + accountability.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the goal of a DHCP starvation attack?
options: Steal the DHCP server's private key
Redirect DNS queries to a rogue resolver
Crash the client's network card
Exhaust the server's address pool so legitimate clients cannot obtain addresses
questions.explanation: The attacker requests leases with many spoofed MACs until the pool is empty, which is a denial of service. Redirecting DNS is the goal of a rogue DHCP server, a different attack that often follows starvation.
questions.concept: Starvation = DoS on the address pool.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which is one of the three essential properties of a firewall?
options: It must run on the same host as the web server
It must block all ICMP
It must decrypt all TLS traffic
All traffic between inside and outside must pass through it (single choke point)
questions.explanation: The properties are: single choke point, only policy-authorised traffic passes, and the firewall itself is hardened. TLS decryption is an optional feature of some products, not a defining property.
questions.concept: Firewall: choke point, policy enforcement, hardened.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does a passive IDS differ from an inline IPS?
options: An IPS can only work offline on pcap files
Both must sit inline
An IDS drops packets; an IPS only logs
An IDS watches a copy of traffic and alerts; an IPS sits in the path and can drop packets
questions.explanation: An IDS on a SPAN port adds no risk to production traffic but cannot block, while an inline IPS can block but may drop legitimate traffic on false positives. The second option reverses the roles.
questions.concept: IDS = out-of-band alerting; IPS = inline prevention.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the maximum period of an L-stage LFSR?
options: 2L
questions.explanation: The all-zero state maps to itself, so at most 2^L - 1 non-zero states are visited before repeating; a primitive feedback polynomial achieves this. 2L is the number of output bits an attacker needs to break the register.
questions.concept: Max LFSR period = 2^L - 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In RSA encryption, which key does each party use?
options: The sender encrypts with the recipient's public key (e, n); the recipient decrypts with the private key (d, n)
The sender encrypts with its own private key; the recipient decrypts with the sender's public key
Both use the same shared secret key
The recipient encrypts with (e, n) and the sender decrypts with (d, n)
questions.explanation: Anyone can encrypt to the public key, but only the holder of d can decrypt. Using the private key on a message is signing, which provides authenticity rather than confidentiality.
questions.concept: Encrypt with public, decrypt with private; sign with private, verify with public.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What three actions can a Security Policy Database (SPD) entry specify?
options: Encrypt, compress, or fragment
Tunnel, transport, or NAT
Discard, bypass IPsec, or apply IPsec
Accept, reject, or log
questions.explanation: Every packet is matched against SPD selectors and is dropped, passed in clear, or protected using an SA from the SAD. Tunnel and transport are modes of applying IPsec, not SPD actions.
questions.concept: SPD = policy (what to do); SAD = parameters (how).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does an EnCase .E01 image protect integrity?
options: Each 32 KB block has its own SHA-256 hash and there is no whole-image hash
Each data chunk carries a checksum (such as Adler-32 or CRC), and one cryptographic hash covers the whole image
The image is encrypted with the examiner's password
Integrity is not protected; only compression is applied
questions.explanation: Per-chunk checksums catch localised corruption cheaply, and an MD5/SHA-1 (or SHA-256) of the acquired data verifies the whole image. The claim of a cryptographic hash for every block is the error the notes correct.
questions.concept: E01: per-chunk checksum + whole-image hash.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A laptop shows a link light, but its address is 169.254.12.7 and no web site loads. Using bottom-up troubleshooting, where is the fault most likely?
options: Layer 3 address configuration: the host never received an address from DHCP
Layer 7: the browser's cache is corrupt
Layer 4: the web server's port 443 is closed
Layer 1: the cable is unplugged
questions.explanation: The link light shows Layer 1 is up, and a 169.254.x.x self-assigned address means automatic configuration failed, so the host has no usable IP setup. Blaming a closed server port skips the lower layer that is already visibly broken.
questions.concept: Troubleshoot bottom-up: link, addressing, ports, application.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: You must split 192.168.10.0/24 into at least 6 equal subnets. What mask results, and how many usable hosts per subnet?
questions.explanation: 2^n >= 6 needs n = 3 borrowed bits, giving /27 with 5 host bits: 32 addresses, 30 usable. /26 only yields 4 subnets, and '32 usable' forgets the network and broadcast addresses.
questions.concept: Borrow n bits: 2^n subnets; remaining h bits: 2^h - 2 hosts.
questions.source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 19

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: During iterative DNS resolution of www.shop.example, which machine sends the query to the .example TLD server?
options: The authoritative server for shop.example
The local DNS resolver
The client's browser
The root server
questions.explanation: In iterative mode the root returns a referral and the local resolver itself follows it to the TLD and then the authoritative server. In recursive mode the root would query onward on the resolver's behalf, which is the tempting confusion.
questions.concept: Iterative = referrals followed by the resolver; recursive = each server asks the next.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In a three-way handshake the client's SYN has Seq = 9,000 and the server's SYN-ACK has Seq = 15,000. What are Seq and Ack in the client's final ACK?
questions.explanation: SYN consumes one sequence number on each side, so the client continues from 9,001 and acknowledges 15,001. Seq = 9,000 forgets that the SYN itself used up 9,000.
questions.concept: SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number; a pure ACK consumes none.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A router drops an ICMP Destination Unreachable message because its queue is full. What does the router send?
options: Nothing: no ICMP error is generated about an ICMP error message
A new Destination Unreachable to the original sender
A Source Quench to the previous hop
A Parameter Problem message to the destination
questions.explanation: Errors about errors could cascade into storms, so ICMP never reports on ICMP error messages. Source Quench is deprecated and, when it was used, it went to the source host, not the previous hop.
questions.concept: No ICMP error for an ICMP error.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: The manager sends nothing, but an attacker injects 'ADD users G, H, I' claiming to be the manager, and the server obeys. How is this best classified?
options: Replay, violating availability
Passive eavesdropping, violating confidentiality
Traffic analysis, violating privacy
Fabrication through masquerade, violating authenticity
questions.explanation: No genuine message existed to replay or modify; the attacker created one under a forged identity. Replay requires a captured genuine message, which is absent here.
questions.concept: Fabrication = forged message under a false identity.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Under a continuous SYN flood that fills the backlog in 0.2 s, an admin cuts the SYN-RECEIVED timeout from 60 s to 10 s. What is the effect?
options: Negligible: the queue still refills within 0.2 s, long before any entry times out
Legitimate clients get guaranteed slots
The backlog doubles in size
The attack stops, because entries expire six times faster
questions.explanation: A timeout only helps if it is shorter than the fill time; at 10 s it is still 50 times longer than 0.2 s. Stateless defences such as SYN cookies, or upstream filtering, are needed instead.
questions.concept: Timeouts do not beat a flood that refills faster than they expire.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A 60-byte DNS query produces a 3,000-byte response. If an attacker sends 10 Mbps of spoofed queries through open resolvers, about how much traffic hits the victim?
options: 500 Mbps
50 Mbps
10 Mbps
3,000 Mbps
questions.explanation: Amplification factor = 3,000 / 60 = 50, so 10 Mbps x 50 = 500 Mbps arrives at the victim. 50 Mbps confuses the factor with the result.
questions.concept: Victim load = attacker rate x amplification factor.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A capture shows segments where tcp[13] == 24 (0x18). Which flags are set?
options: RST and PSH
FIN and ACK
SYN and ACK
PSH and ACK
questions.explanation: Flag values: FIN 0x01, SYN 0x02, RST 0x04, PSH 0x08, ACK 0x10. 0x18 = 0x10 + 0x08. SYN-ACK would be 0x12 = 18.
questions.concept: tcp[13] bits: CWR ECE URG ACK PSH RST SYN FIN.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the multiplicative inverse of 7 modulo 26?
questions.explanation: 7 x 15 = 105 = 4 x 26 + 1, so 15 is the inverse. 19 is the additive inverse (7 + 19 = 26), not the multiplicative one.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: RC4 KSA with key bytes [3, 1, 4] repeated in T. Starting from j = 0 and the identity S, what are S[0..3] after the i = 0 step?
questions.explanation: j = (0 + S[0] + T[0]) mod 256 = 0 + 0 + 3 = 3, then S[0] and S[3] swap, giving [3, 1, 2, 0, ...]. [0, 1, 2, 3] forgets the swap.
questions.concept: Each KSA step: update j, then swap S[i] and S[j].

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In the lab, g = 3, p = 19, Client 1 sends A = 5 and Client 2 sends B = 11. After brute-forcing Client 1's exponent, what key does the relay compute?
questions.explanation: 3^4 mod 19 = 5, so a = 4; K = 11^4 mod 19 = 11. 18 is the figure in the original lab write-up, which used the wrong exponent 6 (11^6 mod 19 = 1).
questions.concept: Recover a by search, then K = B^a mod p.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which IPv4 header field is included in AH's integrity check?
options: Header checksum
Identification
Fragment offset
TTL
questions.explanation: Identification is immutable in transit, so AH covers it; TTL, checksum, DSCP/TOS, flags and fragment offset may change en route and are zeroed for the ICV calculation. Including TTL would make every packet fail verification after one hop.
questions.concept: AH zeroes mutable fields: TTL, checksum, TOS, flags, fragment offset.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Carving finds FF D8 FF starting at offset 0x1000 and the matching FF D9 whose last byte is at offset 0x1A3F. How many bytes is the recovered JPEG?
options: 2,623 bytes
6,719 bytes
2,624 bytes
2,622 bytes
questions.explanation: Size = last offset - first offset + 1 = 0x1A3F - 0x1000 + 1 = 0xA40 = 2,624 bytes. Leaving out the +1 drops the final footer byte.
questions.concept: Inclusive range length = end - start + 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Path A has hops 0.8 then 0.5; path B is a single hop of 0.7. Both reach node X, and a final hop from X to the goal has trust 0.9. What is the overall trust?
questions.explanation: Path A = 0.8 x 0.5 = 0.4; parallel with 0.7 gives 0.4 + 0.7 - 0.28 = 0.82; then x 0.9 = 0.738. 0.820 forgets the final series hop.
questions.concept: Reduce series paths, combine in parallel, then apply remaining series hops.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: You must carve 192.168.50.0/24 into subnets for 100, 50 and 20 hosts without overlap. Which plan is valid?
questions.explanation: Allocating largest first: a /25 (126 hosts) covers .0-.127, a /26 (62 hosts) fits at .128-.191, and a /27 (30 hosts) at .192-.223, all aligned and disjoint. The second plan places .64/26 inside the /25 already given out; the third gives the 100-host LAN a /26 with only 62 usable addresses.
questions.concept: VLSM: allocate largest blocks first, on aligned boundaries, without overlap.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A firm needs to block unsolicited inbound connections, allow outbound web, inspect HTTP for malicious URLs and log users by name. Which design best fits?
options: An application gateway for every protocol and no packet filter
A stateful filter at the perimeter plus an authenticating HTTP proxy (application gateway) for outbound web
A stateless filter alone with rules for ports 80 and 443
DNSSEC on the internal resolver
questions.explanation: Stateful filtering handles connection direction efficiently, and the proxy adds URL inspection and user identity for the one protocol that needs it. A gateway for every protocol multiplies maintenance and latency; DNSSEC does not filter traffic.
questions.concept: Combine packet filtering with targeted application gateways.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: The lab relay can read RC4 chat because DH used p = 19. The team moves to a 2,048-bit p but still does not authenticate half-keys. Which assessment is correct?
options: The relay can still brute-force 2,048-bit exponents in seconds
Passive brute-forcing of the discrete log is now infeasible, but an active relay can still substitute half-keys and read everything
Nothing improves, because DH is broken at any size
The system is now fully secure against the relay
questions.explanation: Large p blocks the passive DLP attack, but MitM does not need any discrete log; it needs only the ability to swap unauthenticated values. Both fixes are needed: large groups and authentication.
questions.concept: Large parameters stop passive attacks; authentication stops active ones.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In practical TCP/IP stacks, where do the OSI session and presentation functions usually end up?
options: They are dropped and no longer performed by any component
They are performed by the network interface card firmware
They are implemented inside the transport layer by TCP
They are absorbed into the application layer (e.g. TLS libraries, cookies, JSON encoding)
questions.explanation: TCP/IP has no separate Layer 5 or 6; applications and their libraries do encryption, encoding and session tracking themselves. TCP provides a reliable byte stream but no encoding, encryption or session semantics, so placing these functions in the transport layer is wrong.
questions.concept: TCP/IP folds OSI Layers 5-7 into a single application layer.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the directed broadcast address of the classful network 20.0.0.0?
questions.explanation: 20.0.0.0 is Class A (/8), so the host part is the last 24 bits; setting them all to 1 gives 20.255.255.255. 20.0.0.255 would be correct only for a /24 network.
questions.concept: Directed broadcast = network ID with every host bit set to 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which DNS record type maps an IP address back to a host name?
options: MX record
PTR (pointer) record
NS record
A record
questions.explanation: Reverse (inverse) DNS uses PTR records. An A record goes the other way, from name to IPv4 address.
questions.concept: A = name to IPv4; PTR = address to name; MX = mail server; NS = name server.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: NS-2 combines which two languages?
options: C for the core and Lua for configuration
Java for the core and Python for scripts
C++ for the simulation core and OTcl for scripting topologies and events
Go for the core and YAML for topologies
questions.explanation: The event scheduler and protocol code are in C++ for speed, and OTcl scripts build topologies without recompiling. Lua configuration belongs to Snort 3, a different tool in this course.
questions.concept: NS-2: C++ core + OTcl scripts; traces viewed in NAM.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which two attacks are passive under X.800?
options: Modification and denial of service
Release of message contents and traffic analysis
Replay and masquerade
Masquerade and traffic analysis
questions.explanation: Passive attacks only observe; the active attacks are masquerade, replay, modification and DoS. Masquerade changes system behaviour by impersonation, so it is active.
questions.concept: Passive = observe; active = alter or disrupt.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why is a rogue DHCP server so dangerous?
options: It can disable the victim's firewall remotely
Its OFFER can set the victim's default gateway and DNS server, enabling man-in-the-middle and pharming
It always crashes the legitimate DHCP server
It can change the victim's MAC address
questions.explanation: Clients accept the first offer, so a rogue server that answers first controls where traffic and name lookups go. It does not need to crash the real server; it just answers faster.
questions.concept: DHCP spoofing -> malicious gateway/DNS -> MitM.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What defines a traditional (stateless) packet filter?
options: It judges each packet in isolation against static header rules, keeping no memory of connections
It tracks every TCP connection in a table
It inspects application payloads for malware
It authenticates users before relaying traffic
questions.explanation: Stateless filters look at addresses, protocol, ports, flags and ICMP type for each packet alone. Connection tables are what make a filter stateful.
questions.concept: Stateless = per-packet; stateful = connection-aware.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Where does BPF filtering happen in a tcpdump capture, and why does it matter?
options: In Wireshark after the capture is saved
In the kernel, so unmatched packets are discarded before being copied to user space
On the remote router
In the NIC firmware only
questions.explanation: Kernel-level filtering keeps capture fast and light at high traffic rates. Wireshark display filters work after capture, which is a different stage.
questions.concept: BPF = in-kernel capture filter.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why is a plain LFSR keystream insecure?
options: It needs a key longer than the message
Its period is always too short to use
It cannot be implemented in hardware
Its feedback is linear, so about 2L known output bits reveal the taps and the internal state
questions.explanation: From 2L consecutive bits an attacker solves linear equations over GF(2) (or runs Berlekamp-Massey) to rebuild the register. Long periods are achievable, so period length is not the flaw.
questions.concept: Linearity, not period, is the LFSR's weakness.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why is unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle?
options: DH only works on prime numbers below 1,000
The generator g is secret and can be stolen
The shared key is sent in clear
Nothing proves who sent each half-key, so an attacker can substitute its own and share a key with each side
questions.explanation: The exchanged values are public, and without signatures or certificates neither party can tell whose half-key arrived. The shared key itself is never transmitted.
questions.concept: Authenticate half-keys to stop DH MitM.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does IPsec tunnel mode add to a packet?
options: A second TCP header
A new outer IP header, so the whole original packet, inner header included, becomes the protected payload
A TLS record header
Nothing; it reuses the original IP header
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode wraps the original datagram in a new IP header between gateways, hiding inner addresses when ESP is used. Transport mode is the one that keeps the original header in front.
questions.concept: Tunnel = new outer header; transport = original header kept.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In the formal model, what is an attack graph?
options: The set of failing executions L(M) \ P, i.e. every execution that violates the security property
A network topology diagram
The set of executions that satisfy the security property
The list of CVEs found by a vulnerability scanner
questions.explanation: Given the model's language L(M) and the safe executions P, the attack graph is what remains: all executions that break P. Scanner output lists isolated bugs, which is exactly what attack graphs go beyond.
questions.concept: Attack graph = L(M) minus P.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which pairing of attack and mitigation is correct?
options: VLAN hopping - upgrade to TLS 1.3
XML external entity injection - enable SYN cookies
Ping flood - set the HttpOnly cookie flag
Session fixation - issue a fresh session ID after login
questions.explanation: Session fixation relies on the victim keeping an attacker-known ID, so regenerating the ID at authentication defeats it. SYN cookies defend TCP handshakes and do nothing about malicious XML parsing; the other pairings are similarly mismatched layers.
questions.concept: Match the control to the layer of the attack.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A router holds the four /26 subnets of 192.168.1.0/24. A packet arrives for 192.168.1.140. Which subnet entry matches after the bitwise AND?
questions.explanation: 140 = 10001100 and the mask octet 192 = 11000000; the AND is 10000000 = 128, so the match is 192.168.1.128. 192.168.1.140 is a host, and routers store networks, not individual hosts.
questions.concept: Routers AND the destination with each mask and compare with stored network IDs.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In iterative resolution, what does a TLD server normally return for a name it does not hold?
options: The final A record of the host
A copy of the root zone
A referral naming the authoritative name server for the domain (with its address as glue)
An error telling the resolver to stop
questions.explanation: TLD servers delegate: they point to the domain's authoritative server rather than answering for the host. Only the authoritative server holds the final A record.
questions.concept: Root -> TLD referral -> authoritative answer.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A sender transmits three 1,000-byte segments with Seq 501, 1,501 and 2,501. The first is lost; the second and third arrive. What ACK does the receiver send?
options: 501 (duplicate ACKs)
questions.explanation: TCP ACKs are cumulative: the receiver still waits for byte 501 and buffers the out-of-order data. 3,501 would acknowledge bytes it has not received contiguously.
questions.concept: Cumulative ACK = next in-order byte expected.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: The notes once said Source Quench is sent from an overloaded router back to the previous router R1. What is correct?
options: It is sent to the destination host to slow the receiver
It is still the standard TCP congestion signal
It is sent to every router on the path
It was sent to the original source host, and it is now deprecated
questions.explanation: ICMP always reports to the source address of the offending datagram, and Source Quench was deprecated in 2012 because it was ineffective and abusable. Modern congestion control uses loss, delay and ECN, not Source Quench.
questions.concept: ICMP messages report to the source; Source Quench is obsolete.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: All traffic to a trading desk is encrypted, yet an observer predicts large trades from bursts of message sizes and timing. What is happening, and what helps?
options: Release of message contents; longer encryption keys
Masquerade; two-factor authentication
Traffic analysis; traffic padding and masking of message sizes and timing
Replay; sequence numbers
questions.explanation: Encryption hides contents but not volume, timing or endpoints; padding and constant-rate traffic hide these patterns. Longer keys strengthen secrecy of contents, which is not what is leaking.
questions.concept: Encryption does not hide metadata; padding does.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A SYN flood spoofs the source address of a host that is online and active. Why does this weaken the attack?
options: The server refuses all SYNs from active hosts
The real host completes the handshake for the attacker
The real host receives an unexpected SYN-ACK and replies with RST, which clears the half-open entry
Routers drop packets from active hosts
questions.explanation: A host that did not send a SYN answers a stray SYN-ACK with RST, freeing the server's memory. That is why attackers use offline addresses or botnets that silently ignore SYN-ACKs.
questions.concept: Live spoofed hosts send RST; floods need silent sources.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A stateless ACL allows 'outside -> 222.22/16, TCP, src port 80, dst port > 1023, ACK set'. An attacker sends such a packet with no prior connection. What happens under stateless and stateful filtering?
options: Both allow it because port 80 is trusted
Stateless allows it; a stateful filter (check-connection) drops it because no matching session exists
Both drop it because the ACK flag is set
Stateless drops it; stateful allows it
questions.explanation: The stateless rule matches on header values alone, so a crafted ACK packet passes; a stateful filter checks its connection table first. Port 80 is not trusted in itself; only connection state proves the packet is a reply.
questions.concept: Only connection state distinguishes real replies from crafted ACKs.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: During an nmap -sS scan, port 22 returns RST and port 445 returns nothing after retries. How does nmap report them?
options: 22 closed, 445 filtered
22 filtered, 445 open
22 open, 445 closed
Both open|filtered
questions.explanation: RST means the host is reachable but nothing listens (closed); silence suggests a firewall dropping probes (filtered). open|filtered is used for scans like UDP or FIN, where silence is ambiguous, not for SYN scans.
questions.concept: SYN scan: SYN-ACK open, RST closed, silence filtered.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Encrypt 'h' with the affine cipher C = (P x k1 + k2) mod 26, where k1 = 5 and k2 = 8.
options: R
X
J
U
questions.explanation: 'h' = 7; 7 x 5 + 8 = 43, mod 26 = 17 = 'R'. Adding before multiplying gives 'X', which applies the steps in the wrong order.
questions.concept: Affine encryption: multiply by k1, then add k2.
questions.source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Cryptography and Network Security, ch. 3

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Continue the KSA with key [3, 1, 4]: after the i = 0 step j = 3. What is j after the i = 1 step?
questions.explanation: S[1] is still 1 and T[1] = 1, so j = (3 + 1 + 1) mod 256 = 5; S[1] and S[5] are then swapped. 2 forgets to carry j forward from the previous step.
questions.concept: j accumulates across KSA iterations.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Mallory sits between Alice and Bob in a DH exchange with p = 29, g = 2. Alice's a = 5; Mallory replaces Bob's value with M = g^3 mod p. Which key does Alice end up sharing, and with whom?
options: 27, shared with Bob
15, shared with Bob
3, shared with nobody
27, shared with Mallory
questions.explanation: Alice computes M^a = 8^5 mod 29 = 27; Mallory computes A^m to get the same value. Bob never saw Alice's real half-key, so he cannot share this key with her.
questions.concept: In DH MitM, each victim shares a key with the attacker.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why does AH fail through a NAT router?
options: NAT strips the AH header
AH encrypts the IP header, which NAT cannot read
NAT drops all packets with protocol 51
NAT rewrites the source IP (and ports with PAT), which AH's ICV covers, so verification fails
questions.explanation: AH authenticates immutable header fields including addresses, and NAT must change them. AH does not encrypt anything, so the third option is wrong.
questions.concept: AH and NAT are incompatible.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A JPEG displays normally, but a hex editor shows several kilobytes after the FF D9 footer. What is the most likely explanation?
options: LSB steganography in the pixel values
A corrupted file header
Normal JPEG compression overhead
Data appended after the end-of-image marker (append-style hiding); viewers stop rendering at FF D9
questions.explanation: Image viewers ignore bytes after EOI, so appended data is invisible on screen but obvious in hex. LSB hiding changes pixel bits within the image data and adds nothing after the footer.
questions.concept: Check for data after the footer.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A student script computes the parallel trust of 0.72 and 0.10 as 0.72 + 0.10 = 0.82. What is wrong?
options: It should take the larger value, 0.72
It should multiply: 0.72 x 0.10 = 0.072
It omits the overlap term; the correct value is 0.72 + 0.10 - 0.072 = 0.748
Nothing; parallel trust is a simple sum
questions.explanation: The OR formula subtracts the probability that both succeed, otherwise sums can exceed 1. Multiplying gives the series (AND) result, which applies to sequential hops.
questions.concept: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A)P(B).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which set of four /24 networks can be summarised by a single /22 route?
questions.explanation: A /22 spans four /24s and must start on a third-octet multiple of 4; 4-7 starts at 4, so 200.1.4.0/22 covers them exactly. 2-5 also has four networks, but 2 is not a multiple of 4, so no single /22 covers them without including 0-1 or 6-7.
questions.concept: Aggregation obeys the same rules as CIDR: power-of-two count and alignment.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: You must harden a recursive resolver against off-path cache poisoning. Which combination is the strongest correct design?
options: Random 16-bit transaction IDs, random source ports, bailiwick filtering of glue, and DNSSEC validation
Blocking UDP 53 and allowing only ICMP
Random IDs only, and caching all glue for speed
Sequential IDs with a fixed source port, but a longer TTL
questions.explanation: Randomness expands the guessing space to about 2^32, bailiwick checks stop glue injection, and DNSSEC rejects forged data. Longer TTLs keep a poisoned record alive for longer, so they make the problem worse.
questions.concept: Layered DNS hardening: entropy, bailiwick, signatures.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Design the key exchange for the chat app so that neither passive nor active relays can read messages. Which design is sound?
options: RSA where the server sends its public key unsigned and the client uses it at once
Ephemeral DH (or ECDHE) over a large standard group, with each half-key signed by a certificate-backed key the peer verifies, then a KDF to derive session keys
Static DH with p = 19, with the shared key sent in clear for confirmation
Hard-code one RC4 key in both clients and skip key exchange
questions.explanation: Ephemeral DH gives forward secrecy, signatures bind half-keys to identities, and a KDF produces proper session keys. A hard-coded key is shared by every installation and cannot be changed once it leaks.
questions.concept: Authenticated ephemeral DH + KDF.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What are the two sublayers of the data link layer?
options: ARP and RARP
Logical Link Control (LLC) and Media Access Control (MAC)
Media Access Control (MAC) and Internet Protocol (IP)
Logical Link Control (LLC) and Physical Coding (PHY)
questions.explanation: LLC is the upper sublayer that interfaces with the network layer; MAC is the lower sublayer that handles hardware addressing and medium access. PHY coding belongs to the physical layer, and ARP is a helper protocol, not a sublayer.
questions.concept: Data link = LLC (upper) + MAC (lower).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Under classful addressing, what fraction of the IPv4 space is Class C?
options: 12.5% (2^29 addresses)
50% (2^31 addresses)
6.25% (2^28 addresses)
25% (2^30 addresses)
questions.explanation: Successive halving gives A = 1/2, B = 1/4, C = 1/8 and D and E 1/16 each. 25% is Class B's share.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: HTTP is stateless. How do web applications keep a user logged in across requests?
options: With cookies or session tokens sent on each request
By storing state in the IP header
By keeping one TCP connection open forever
Through the DNS cache
questions.explanation: The server treats each request independently, so it issues a cookie or token that the browser returns with every request. Persistent connections reduce handshakes but are not a session mechanism; a new connection would lose the 'state'.
questions.concept: State on top of stateless HTTP comes from cookies and tokens.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How are ARP requests and replies delivered?
options: Request by broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF); reply by unicast to the requester
Both by broadcast
Request by unicast to the gateway; reply by broadcast
Request by multicast; reply by broadcast
questions.explanation: The asker does not know the target MAC, so it broadcasts; only the owner of the IP answers, directly to the asker's MAC. 'Multicast request, broadcast reply' is a known slide error that the notes correct.
questions.concept: ARP: who-has = broadcast; is-at = unicast.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which list contains only X.800 active attacks?
options: Release of contents, replay, masquerade, DoS
Masquerade, traffic analysis, modification, DoS
Eavesdropping, traffic analysis, replay, DoS
Masquerade, replay, modification of messages, denial of service
questions.explanation: Each of the four alters data or disrupts service. Traffic analysis and release of contents are passive, so any list containing them is wrong.
questions.concept: Active attacks: masquerade, replay, modification, DoS.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why is a TCP SYN flood called a half-open attack?
options: The attacker sends SYNs but never completes the handshake, leaving entries stuck in the server's backlog
It targets only half of the server's ports
The server closes one direction of each connection with FIN
Only half of each packet is transmitted
questions.explanation: SYN and SYN-ACK are exchanged, but the final ACK never comes, so half-open entries pile up until the queue is full. Half-close with FIN is graceful teardown, unrelated to flooding.
questions.concept: SYN flood exhausts the half-open (SYN backlog) queue.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What can an application gateway do that packet filters cannot?
options: Filter by source IP address
Drop packets with the SYN flag set
Make decisions on application data, such as authenticating users before relaying their sessions
Filter on destination port numbers
questions.explanation: A proxy terminates the application session, so it can check usernames, commands or URLs. Port, flag and address filtering are standard packet-filter abilities.
questions.concept: Application gateways decide on Layer 7 data.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does Kerckhoffs' principle state?
options: Keys must be at least 128 bits long
A cipher should stay secure even if everything except the key is public
The algorithm must be kept secret to be secure
Ciphertext should be longer than the plaintext
questions.explanation: Security should rest on a replaceable key, because secret algorithms leak and cannot easily be changed. A key-length rule is a separate practical guideline, not the principle.
questions.concept: Public algorithm, secret key.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How are RC4's arrays S and T initialised before key scheduling?
options: S is filled with the key; T with zeros
Both arrays are filled with random bytes
S[i] = i for i = 0..255; T is filled by repeating the key bytes
questions.explanation: S starts as the identity permutation and T[i] = K[i mod keylen]. RC4 does not use random fill; all randomness comes from the key.
questions.concept: RC4 init: S identity, T repeated key.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the minimum RSA modulus size generally recommended today?
options: 2,048 bits
1,024 bits
128 bits
512 bits
questions.explanation: 2,048-bit moduli are the common minimum, with 3,072-4,096 bits for long-lived or high-value keys. 512-bit keys have been factored and 1,024 bits is considered too weak.
questions.concept: RSA >= 2,048 bits.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Where do TLS and IPsec operate, and what follows from that?
options: TLS sits above TCP in each application; IPsec sits at the IP layer in the OS or gateway, protecting all IP traffic without changing applications
TLS sits in the kernel and IPsec in each application
Both sit at the data link layer
IPsec sits above TCP and requires every application to be modified
questions.explanation: Applications must use TLS libraries, while IPsec is configured in the stack or gateway and protects any protocol over IP. The third option reverses the deployment trade-off.
questions.concept: TLS: per application; IPsec: per host or gateway.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the 3-tuple of the formal attack model?
options: M = (P, C, K): plaintexts, ciphertexts and keys
M = (H, C, T): hosts, connectivity and trust
M = (S, tau, s0): state space, transition relation and initial state
M = (E, D, N): intruder, defender and network only
questions.explanation: S is the global state space, tau the allowed transitions and s0 the start state. (H, C, T) are inputs describing the network, and (E, D, N) are the agent classes whose states form S.
questions.concept: Finite-state model: (S, tau, s0).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Traffic to a permitted web server on TCP 443 carries SQL injection in POST bodies. Why can a classic Layer 3/4 firewall not stop it?
options: Layer 3/4 firewalls cannot see port numbers
SQL injection uses UDP, which firewalls do not filter
SQL injection spoofs the source MAC address
It decides on addresses, ports and flags only, so it cannot inspect application payload logic
questions.explanation: The packets are legitimate at Layers 3 and 4 (right address, right port), so a header-based filter passes them; only a WAF or deep inspection that understands HTTP can see the malicious payload. Saying such firewalls cannot see ports is false: ports are exactly what they filter on.
questions.concept: Application-layer attacks need application-aware defences (WAF, DPI).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Is 100.1.2.40 to 100.1.2.55 a valid CIDR block?
options: No: it has 16 addresses, but 40 is not a multiple of 16
No: 16 is not a power of 2
questions.explanation: The range is contiguous and holds 55 - 40 + 1 = 16 = 2^4 addresses, but alignment fails because 40 mod 16 = 8 (in binary the last four bits of 40 are 1000, not 0000). Calling it 100.1.2.40/28 ignores the alignment rule; the /28 containing .40 is 100.1.2.32/28.
questions.concept: Alignment: the first address must have all host bits zero.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A client times out and resends the same request twice. Which method can be retried without risk of creating duplicate records?
options: CONNECT to a proxy
TRACE to the server
POST to a collection
PUT to a specific URI
questions.explanation: PUT is idempotent: repeating it leaves the resource in the same state. POST is non-idempotent, so a retry may add a second record.
questions.concept: Idempotent methods: GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE; POST is not.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A client sends FIN with Seq = 4,000 and Ack = 7,000. What acknowledgement number does the server's ACK carry?
questions.explanation: FIN consumes one sequence number, so the server acknowledges 4,000 + 1 = 4,001. 7,001 confuses the server's own sequence space with the client's.
questions.concept: FIN consumes 1 sequence number.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In which case is an ICMP error message generated?
options: A datagram sent to a broadcast address is discarded
A unicast datagram's TTL reaches 0 at a router
A non-first fragment of a datagram is discarded
An ICMP Time Exceeded message is itself discarded
questions.explanation: The exceptions are errors about ICMP errors, non-first fragments, and multicast/broadcast or special addresses; ordinary unicast TTL expiry is the standard trigger. Broadcast-addressed datagrams are excluded so that one bad packet cannot trigger a flood of replies.
questions.concept: ICMP error exceptions: ICMP errors, non-first fragments, broadcast/multicast.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which X.800 mechanism is essential for non-repudiation of origin?
options: Routing control
Traffic padding
Symmetric encipherment alone
Digital signature (supported by data-integrity mechanisms and notarisation)
questions.explanation: Only the signer holds the private key, so a third party can verify who signed. With a shared symmetric key either party could have produced the message, so it cannot prove origin.
questions.concept: Non-repudiation needs asymmetric signatures, not shared keys.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A DHCP server sits behind a router with a relay agent. Why can it not stop starvation by limiting leases per source MAC in the Ethernet header?
options: Every relayed request arrives with the router's MAC as the frame source; the server must check CHADDR in the DHCP payload instead
Limiting MACs is forbidden by the DHCP standard
Relay agents encrypt the Ethernet header
DHCP requests carry no MAC address at all
questions.explanation: Layer 2 source addresses are rewritten at each hop, so the server only sees the router; the client's hardware address travels inside the DHCP message (CHADDR). DHCP messages do carry the client MAC, just not in the outer frame.
questions.concept: Across routers, judge the DHCP payload (CHADDR), not the frame header.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Policy: internal hosts may open TCP connections out, but outsiders may not open connections in. Which stateless rule implements this?
options: Drop inbound packets with source port above 1023
Drop inbound TCP packets with ACK = 1
Drop inbound TCP packets with ACK = 0 (connection-opening SYNs)
Drop all outbound TCP packets with SYN = 1
questions.explanation: The first packet of any TCP connection has SYN = 1 and ACK = 0; everything after has ACK = 1. Dropping inbound ACK = 1 packets would break replies to connections that insiders opened.
questions.concept: Opening segment = SYN without ACK.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An nmap ACK scan (-sA) gets RST back from ports 80 and 443. What does that show?
options: A firewall is dropping the probes
The ports are unfiltered: probes reach the host, but open/closed is not determined
The ports are closed
The ports are open
questions.explanation: An ACK scan maps firewall rules: RST means the packet got through. It cannot tell open from closed, because both answer an unsolicited ACK with RST.
questions.concept: ACK scan answers 'filtered or not', not 'open or not'.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Decrypt 'W' from an affine cipher with k1 = 7, k2 = 3. (7^-1 mod 26 = 15.)
options: z
p
d
l
questions.explanation: P = (C - k2) x k1^-1 = (22 - 3) x 15 = 285, mod 26 = 25 = 'z'. Multiplying by k1 instead of its inverse re-encrypts rather than decrypts.
questions.concept: Affine decryption: subtract k2, then multiply by k1^-1.

questions.subject: Networking
