questions.stem: A toy RC4 works modulo 8 (S has 8 entries, all arithmetic mod 8) with key [1, 2, 3, 6]. After the full KSA, what are the first two keystream values?
questions.explanation: Running the 8-step KSA and then two PRGA steps (i = i + 1, j = j + S[i], swap, output S[S[i] + S[j]]) gives 5, 1. Swapping the order of outputs is a typical slip when the PRGA swap is done after the output instead of before.
questions.concept: PRGA order: increment i, update j, swap, then output.
questions.source: Scenario type: Stallings, Network Security Essentials, ch. 2

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: RSA key generation with p = 11, q = 13 and e = 7. What is the private exponent d?
questions.explanation: n = 143, phi(n) = 10 x 12 = 120; d = e^-1 mod phi(n) = 103, since 7 x 103 = 721 = 6 x 120 + 1. Inverting e modulo n instead of phi(n) gives a different, wrong value.
questions.concept: d = e^-1 mod phi(n), with phi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1).
questions.source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Cryptography and Network Security, ch. 10

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why does plain ESP have trouble crossing a PAT (port-translating) router, and what fixes it?
options: ESP needs TCP; switch to TCP port 50
ESP's ICV covers the outer IP header; disable the ICV
PAT drops encrypted packets; turn off encryption
ESP carries no transport ports for PAT to map; NAT-Traversal wraps ESP in UDP port 4500
questions.explanation: PAT tells flows apart by ports, which are hidden inside ESP's encrypted payload; NAT-T adds a UDP header it can translate. ESP's ICV does not cover the outer IP header, which is why it tolerates address rewriting once ports are solved.
questions.concept: ESP through PAT needs NAT-T (UDP 4500).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An 800x600 24-bit RGB image hides 1 bit in the least significant bit of each colour channel. What is the maximum hidden payload?
options: 360,000 bytes
60,000 bytes
180,000 bytes
questions.explanation: 800 x 600 pixels x 3 channels = 1,440,000 bits = 180,000 bytes. 1,440,000 is the bit count, not bytes.
questions.concept: LSB capacity = pixels x channels x bits per channel / 8.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In the DMZ case study, the chain is: web-server buffer overflow -> proxy port scan -> chat-client remote-to-user exploit -> local setuid buffer overflow. Which step raises the intruder's privilege on the Linux database host from user to root?
options: The proxy port scan
The web-server buffer overflow
The local setuid buffer overflow
The chat-client remote-to-user exploit
questions.explanation: The remote-to-user exploit gives a user shell on Linux, and the local setuid overflow escalates that to root. The port scan only changes knowledge (scan = true), not privilege.
questions.concept: Each action rule has privilege and knowledge pre- and post-conditions.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A results portal expects 50,000 users in a burst, each loading a page with 30 small objects. Which connection strategy is best justified?
options: Non-persistent HTTP/1.0 with more server threads, so each object gets a fresh connection
Turn off browser caching so every object stays current
Persistent HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with a short idle timeout, cutting handshakes from about 30 to 1 per user
Disable TCP and serve HTTP/1.0 over raw UDP
questions.explanation: With 30 objects per page, non-persistent HTTP multiplies handshakes and socket churn about 30-fold; keep-alive reuses one connection, and an idle timeout frees sockets promptly. Adding threads to the non-persistent design just pays the handshake cost more times in parallel.
questions.concept: Persistent connections reduce latency and server socket churn.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A SOC wants to detect SYN floods on a busy payment network without any risk of dropping legitimate transactions. Which deployment is best?
options: An nmap -sS scan of the payment servers every minute
Passive Snort IDS on a SPAN/mirror port with threshold-based alert rules feeding the SIEM
tcpdump with -A on the payment server itself
Inline Snort IPS with drop rules on every SYN
questions.explanation: Out-of-band monitoring gives visibility with no chance of blocking real traffic, and thresholds turn floods into alerts. Inline drop rules on SYNs would block legitimate connections, which breaks the stated constraint.
questions.concept: When availability is paramount, detect out-of-band first.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A remote employee behind a café's NAT needs encrypted access to internal servers, with internal addresses hidden. Which configuration is best justified?
options: ESP transport mode without NAT-T, because ESP's ICV ignores the IP header
AH transport mode, because it authenticates every header field
AH tunnel mode, because tunnelling hides addresses
ESP tunnel mode with authentication, negotiated by IKE with NAT-Traversal (UDP 4500)
questions.explanation: ESP gives confidentiality and integrity, tunnel mode hides internal addressing, and NAT-T lets the café's PAT handle the traffic. AH breaks across NAT and provides no encryption.
questions.concept: Remote-access VPN = ESP tunnel + NAT-T.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which of these attacks operates at the physical layer?
options: SQL injection
Radio-frequency jamming of a Wi-Fi access point
TCP SYN flood
ARP cache poisoning
questions.explanation: Jamming drowns legitimate signals in RF noise, so it attacks the medium itself. ARP poisoning is a Layer 2 attack on address mapping, and a SYN flood exhausts Layer 4 connection state, so neither touches raw signals.
questions.concept: Layer 1 threats are physical: jamming, wiretapping, cable cuts, theft.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How many usable host addresses does a /26 subnet provide?
questions.explanation: A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 addresses, minus the network and directed-broadcast addresses = 62. 64 forgets that those two addresses cannot be assigned to hosts.
questions.concept: Usable hosts = 2^h - 2, where h = number of host bits.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What are the minimum and maximum lengths of a TCP header?
options: 8 bytes minimum, 20 bytes maximum
20 bytes minimum, 40 bytes maximum
20 bytes minimum, 60 bytes maximum
32 bytes minimum, 64 bytes maximum
questions.explanation: The fixed part is 20 bytes and options can add up to 40, so the maximum is 60 (HLEN is 4 bits counting 32-bit words: 15 x 4 = 60). 40 bytes is the options limit, not the header maximum.
questions.concept: TCP header = 20 + options (0-40) bytes.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What mapping does ARP perform?
options: A port number to a process ID
A host name to an IP address
A known IPv4 address to the matching MAC address on the local link
A MAC address to an IP address assigned by a server
questions.explanation: ARP resolves the hardware address needed to frame a packet for a local next hop. Assigning IP addresses for a known MAC is what BOOTP/DHCP do.
questions.concept: ARP: IP -> MAC; BOOTP/DHCP: MAC -> IP configuration.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does non-repudiation provide?
options: Assurance that a message stays secret in transit
Hiding the traffic pattern between two hosts
Proof that prevents a sender or receiver from later denying that a message was sent or received
Assurance that a service stays available under load
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation of origin proves who sent a message; of delivery, that it was received. Secrecy in transit is confidentiality, a different service.
questions.concept: Non-repudiation = undeniable proof of origin or delivery.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How do SYN cookies protect a server?
options: The server doubles the backlog for each attack
The server keeps no state for a SYN and encodes connection details in its ISN, rebuilding state only when a valid ACK returns
The server blocks every SYN that carries options
The server sends a browser cookie with each SYN-ACK
questions.explanation: The cookie (a keyed hash of addresses, ports, time and MSS) lives in the SYN-ACK's sequence number, so a flood consumes no memory. It has nothing to do with HTTP cookies despite the name.
questions.concept: SYN cookies = stateless handshake until the final ACK.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is bailiwick checking in a DNS resolver?
options: Limiting the number of queries per client
Verifying the root server's certificate
Discarding glue records for domains unrelated to the zone that was queried
Checking that a reply arrives before the TTL expires
questions.explanation: A server authoritative for one zone should not be trusted to supply addresses for unrelated domains; filtering such glue stops cross-domain poisoning. Root servers do not present certificates in plain DNS.
questions.concept: Trust glue only within the queried zone's bailiwick.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which cryptanalysis model gives the attacker the most power?
options: Known-plaintext attack
Chosen-ciphertext attack (decryption oracle)
Ciphertext-only attack
Chosen-plaintext attack
questions.explanation: In increasing order of power: ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext. Chosen-plaintext gives an encryption oracle; chosen-ciphertext adds the ability to get chosen ciphertexts decrypted.
questions.concept: COA < KPA < CPA < CCA.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which describes RC4?
options: A 64-bit block cipher with 16 rounds
A byte-oriented stream cipher with a variable key length of about 40 to 256 bits
A public-key algorithm based on factoring
A hash function producing 128-bit digests
questions.explanation: RC4 outputs one keystream byte per step and accepts variable-length keys. 64-bit blocks with 16 rounds describes DES.
questions.concept: RC4 = byte-wise stream cipher.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why does a client add random padding (such as OAEP) before RSA-encrypting a short message?
options: To convert RSA into a stream cipher
To make the ciphertext shorter
So the same plaintext encrypts to different ciphertexts and textbook-RSA structure is hidden
To replace the need for a private key
questions.explanation: Textbook RSA is deterministic, so an attacker can test guesses; random padding makes each encryption unique and blocks several algebraic attacks. Padding makes the block fuller, not shorter.
questions.concept: Never use textbook RSA; pad with OAEP.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the role of IKE in IPsec?
options: It compresses headers for low-bandwidth links
It encrypts each data packet
It assigns IP addresses to VPN clients
It authenticates peers and negotiates the security associations and session keys, using Diffie-Hellman
questions.explanation: IKE does the control-plane work in two phases; AH and ESP then protect the data. Packet encryption itself is ESP's job.
questions.concept: IKE = key management; AH/ESP = packet protection.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which three agent classes make up the state space?
options: Client, server and router
E (intruder), D (defender/IDS) and N (network system)
Attacker, victim and ISP
Hosts, ports and services
questions.explanation: The global state is the product of intruder, defender and network states. Hosts and ports are parts of the network model N, not separate agents.
questions.concept: Agents: E, D, N.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An application hands 1,000 bytes to TCP. TCP adds a 20-byte header, IP a 20-byte header, and Ethernet a 14-byte header plus a 4-byte FCS. How many bytes is the Ethernet frame (excluding preamble)?
options: 1,062 bytes
1,054 bytes
1,058 bytes
1,040 bytes
questions.explanation: 1,000 + 20 (TCP) + 20 (IP) + 14 (Ethernet header) + 4 (FCS) = 1,058. 1,054 forgets the FCS trailer, which data-link framing adds at the end.
questions.concept: Encapsulation adds a header at each layer and a trailer at Layer 2.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An organisation needs 1,000 host addresses in one block. What is the smallest suitable CIDR prefix?
options: /22 (1,024 addresses, 1,022 usable)
/21 (2,048 addresses)
/24 (256 addresses)
/23 (512 addresses)
questions.explanation: 2^10 = 1,024 is the smallest power of two that covers 1,000 hosts plus network and broadcast, so 32 - 10 = /22. /21 also works but wastes about 1,000 addresses, which is the waste CIDR was designed to avoid.
questions.concept: Pick the smallest 2^h with 2^h - 2 >= hosts; prefix = 32 - h.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why do many production servers disable the HTTP TRACE method?
options: It echoes the request, which can enable cross-site tracing that exposes headers such as cookies
It opens a TCP tunnel through the proxy
It forces HTTP/1.0 non-persistent connections
It permanently deletes resources
questions.explanation: TRACE reflects the received request back in the response body; combined with scripting it can reveal sensitive headers (XST). Opening a tunnel is CONNECT's job, not TRACE's.
questions.concept: Disable unneeded methods: TRACE risks XST.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which call order is correct for a TCP server in C?
options: socket -> bind -> listen -> accept -> recv/send -> close
socket -> connect -> bind -> accept -> close
bind -> socket -> accept -> listen -> send
socket -> listen -> bind -> recv -> accept
questions.explanation: The server creates the endpoint, binds it to a local address and port, marks it passive, then accepts clients and exchanges data. connect() is the client's call.
questions.concept: Server: socket, bind, listen, accept; client: socket, connect.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A client on subnet 3 needs DHCP but the only server is on subnet 1, beyond a router. How does its DISCOVER reach the server?
options: The server polls every subnet for new MAC addresses
The client sends DISCOVER directly to the server's IP
The router floods 255.255.255.255 to every subnet
A relay agent on subnet 3 receives the broadcast and forwards it to the server as unicast
questions.explanation: Routers do not forward limited broadcasts, so a relay agent (often the router interface) converts it into a unicast to the known server address. Flooding broadcasts across routers is exactly what routers are designed to prevent.
questions.concept: Relay agent: local broadcast in, unicast to the server out.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An e-mail recipient wants assurance about who originated a message; there is no live session between the parties. Which X.800 authentication service fits?
options: Peer-entity authentication
Access control
Data-origin authentication
Availability service
questions.explanation: Peer-entity authentication is used during connection set-up and data transfer; e-mail is connectionless, so the relevant service validates the origin of each data unit. Access control limits who can use resources, a different service.
questions.concept: Connectionless -> data-origin authentication; connection -> peer-entity.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does 'ettercap -T -i eth0 -M arp:remote /192.168.1.1// /192.168.1.50//' do?
options: Runs text-mode, two-way ARP poisoning between the gateway 192.168.1.1 and the host 192.168.1.50 on eth0
Sends a DHCP starvation flood from eth0
Launches a GUI and saves a pcap of all hosts
Scans ports 1 to 50 on the gateway
questions.explanation: -T selects text mode, -i the interface, and -M arp:remote poisons both targets so traffic between them passes through the attacker. GUI mode would be -G and saving traffic would need -w.
questions.concept: Ettercap: -T text, -G GUI, -M arp:remote two-way MitM.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which rule stops outsiders mapping the internal network with traceroute?
options: Drop outgoing ICMP Time Exceeded messages
Drop incoming TCP RST
Drop outgoing DNS queries
Drop incoming ICMP Echo Reply
questions.explanation: Traceroute learns each hop from Time Exceeded replies, so suppressing them hides internal routers. Blocking incoming Echo Replies would break insiders' own ping, not outsiders' mapping.
questions.concept: Traceroute relies on Time Exceeded.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A student without root rights must scan a lab host's TCP ports. Which scan type will nmap use?
options: UDP scan (-sU)
SYN scan (-sS)
OS fingerprinting (-O)
TCP connect scan (-sT) using the operating system's connect() call
questions.explanation: Raw packet crafting for -sS needs privileges, so non-root nmap falls back to full connect() handshakes. -sU and -O also require raw sockets.
questions.concept: Unprivileged nmap = connect scan.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A keyed transposition uses blocks of 4 and key [2 4 1 3], meaning output position 1 takes input character 2, position 2 takes character 4, and so on. Encrypt 'SAFEHOUS'.
options: AESFOSHU
FSEAUHSO
ESAFSUHO
SUOHEFAS
questions.explanation: Block SAFE -> S(2)=A, (4)=E, (1)=S, (3)=F -> AESF; block HOUS -> OSHU. Result AESFOSHU. 'FSEAUHSO' applies the inverse permutation [3 1 4 2], which is what the receiver uses to decrypt.
questions.concept: Apply the permutation within each block; decrypt with its inverse.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: With the key 'Key' (ASCII), standard RC4 produces first keystream byte 0xEB. What is the first ciphertext byte for the plaintext 'P' (0x50)?
options: 0xBB
0xEB
0x9B
0x3B
questions.explanation: 0xEB XOR 0x50 = 0xBB. Adding the bytes (0x3B) is not how a stream cipher combines keystream and plaintext.
questions.concept: Ciphertext byte = plaintext byte XOR keystream byte.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Using the public key (e, n) = (7, 143), encrypt m = 9.
questions.explanation: c = m^e mod n = 9^7 mod 143 = 48. Reducing modulo phi(n) instead of n gives 9; phi(n) is used only to find d.
questions.concept: c = m^e mod n.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An IPsec receiver's anti-replay window currently covers sequence numbers 50-80. Packet 55 arrives for the first time, then 55 again, then 42, then 85. What happens to each?
options: 55 accepted twice; 42 and 85 discarded
All four accepted
55 accepted; 55 again discarded; 42 discarded; 85 accepted and the window slides forward
55 discarded; 42 accepted; 85 discarded
questions.explanation: New numbers inside the window are accepted once and marked; duplicates and numbers left of the window are dropped; numbers to the right are accepted after the ICV checks and advance the window. Discarding 85 would block normal traffic as the sender's counter grows.
questions.concept: Anti-replay: accept once, reject duplicates and stale numbers, slide right.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Entropy analysis gives 7.98 bits per byte for a file named notes.txt. What does this suggest?
options: A file full of zeros
An empty file
The content is probably encrypted or compressed, inconsistent with plain text, so it should be examined further
Normal English text
questions.explanation: Entropy runs from 0 to 8 bits per byte; values near 8 mean near-random bytes, typical of ciphertext or compressed data. English text usually sits around 4-5 bits per byte.
questions.concept: High entropy flags encryption, packing or compression.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An IDS watches the link from the DMZ web server to the Linux host, so the attacker pivots via the internal Windows host. Both the direct and the pivot paths use the chat-client exploit on Linux. What is the single most effective fix?
options: Add a second IDS on the same DMZ-to-Linux link
Patch or block the chat-client service on the Linux host, since every path depends on it
Patch only the Windows host
Block port 80 on the internal firewall only
questions.explanation: An action shared by all paths forms a hitting set of size one, so removing it cuts every path. Patching Windows only removes the pivot path; the direct path still exists, though it would trigger an alarm.
questions.concept: Look for actions common to all attack paths.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A file server must handle 1,000 near-simultaneous clients but serve at most 100 transfers at once. Which design is sound?
options: Use one UDP broadcast socket so every client receives the file at once
Create 1,000 listening sockets, each bound to the same port, one per client
Let each child process call bind() and listen() again on the server port
One listening socket with a backlog; an accept loop hands each data socket to a worker pool of 100 (processes or threads); the parent closes its copy of the data socket and reaps finished children
questions.explanation: A single passive socket queues connections, accept() yields per-client sockets, and a bounded pool caps concurrency; closing unused descriptors and reaping children avoids leaks and zombies. Binding many sockets to one port (without special options) fails with 'address in use' and gives no concurrency control.
questions.concept: Concurrency = one listener + per-client data sockets + bounded workers.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which Snort rule correctly alerts on ICMP echo requests from outside networks to the home network?
options: alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET 8 (msg:"Inbound ping"; sid:1000010; rev:1;)
drop icmp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"Inbound ping"; itype:8; sid:10; rev:1;)
alert icmp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"Inbound ping"; itype:0; sid:1000010; rev:1;)
alert icmp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET any (msg:"Inbound ping"; itype:8; sid:1000010; rev:1;)
questions.explanation: Echo Request is ICMP type 8, direction runs external to home, and local rules use sid >= 1,000,000. Type 0 is Echo Reply; the drop version reverses direction, uses a reserved low sid, and only works inline.
questions.concept: Get protocol, direction, ICMP type and local SID range right.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A hospital group must encrypt traffic from 25 legacy applications between four sites over the Internet, and the applications cannot be modified. Which approach is best?
options: Add TLS to each of the 25 applications
Rely on the ISP's network being private
AH transport mode on every server
IPsec ESP tunnels between site gateways, with SPD rules selecting inter-site traffic
questions.explanation: IPsec at the gateways protects all IP traffic transparently, which suits applications that cannot change. TLS would need code changes in every application, and AH does not encrypt.
questions.concept: No application changes possible -> network-layer protection.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which OSI layer is known as the 'syntax layer' because it handles translation, compression and encryption of data formats?
options: Session layer
Data link layer
Application layer
Presentation layer
questions.explanation: The presentation layer standardises data representation (character sets, serialisation, compression, encryption). The session layer manages dialogues and checkpoints rather than data syntax.
questions.concept: Layer 6 = data representation: translate, compress, encrypt.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for a range of addresses to form a valid CIDR block?
options: The block must begin on an octet boundary such as /8, /16 or /24
The addresses must be contiguous
The number of addresses must be a power of 2
The first address must be divisible by the block size
questions.explanation: CIDR exists precisely to free prefixes from octet boundaries; any length from /1 to /32 is allowed. The other three are the actual validity rules: contiguity, power-of-two size and alignment.
questions.concept: CIDR rules: contiguous, size 2^n, first address a multiple of the block size.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How long is the UDP header?
options: 16 bytes
20 bytes
4 bytes
8 bytes
questions.explanation: UDP has four 16-bit fields (source port, destination port, length, checksum) = 8 bytes. 20 bytes is the minimum TCP or IPv4 header.
questions.concept: UDP header: 4 fields x 16 bits = 8 bytes.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which UDP ports do BOOTP and DHCP use?
options: Client 67, server 68
Client 68, server 67
Client 53, server 53
Client 546, server 547
questions.explanation: Both protocols run over UDP with the client on 68 and the server on 67. 546/547 are the DHCPv6 ports, and 53 is DNS.
questions.concept: DHCP/BOOTP: UDP 68 (client) -> 67 (server).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which three things does the X.800 security architecture define?
options: Security attacks, security services and security mechanisms
Physical, logical and administrative controls
Keys, certificates and passwords
Firewalls, routers and switches
questions.explanation: X.800 relates attacks (what threatens), services (what protection is needed) and mechanisms (how it is implemented) to the OSI layers. Keys and certificates are mechanisms in use, not the framework's structure.
questions.concept: X.800: attack -> service -> mechanism.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) check?
options: IP source addresses against the routing table
DNS replies against DNSSEC signatures
ARP packets against the trusted DHCP snooping binding table, dropping forged replies
TCP sequence numbers against a random window
questions.explanation: DAI uses the IP-to-MAC-to-port bindings learned by DHCP snooping to validate ARP at the switch. Checking source IPs against routes is uRPF, a Layer 3 control.
questions.concept: DAI + DHCP snooping stop ARP spoofing at the switch.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does the tcpdump option -nn do?
options: Enables promiscuous mode twice
Disables both host-name and port-name resolution
Prints payloads in hexadecimal
Captures only n packets
questions.explanation: -n stops DNS look-ups and -nn also stops port-name translation, which speeds capture and avoids leaking queries. Counting packets is -c.
questions.concept: -nn = numeric output only.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: The Caesar cipher is the additive cipher with which key?
questions.explanation: Caesar shifts each letter three places (hello -> KHOOR). k = 13 is ROT13, and k = 26 is equivalent to 0, which leaves the text unchanged.
questions.concept: Additive cipher: C = (P + k) mod 26.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the update step in RC4's key-scheduling algorithm (KSA)?
options: j = (j + S[i]) mod 256, then output S[j]
j = S[i] XOR T[i], with no swap
j = (j + S[i] + T[i]) mod 256, then swap S[i] and S[j]
i = (i + 1) mod 256, then XOR S[i] with the key
questions.explanation: The KSA runs i from 0 to 255, mixing key bytes via T into j and swapping. j = (j + S[i]) mod 256 without T belongs to the PRGA.
questions.concept: KSA uses T; PRGA does not.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which values in a Diffie-Hellman exchange are public?
options: a, b and K
The shared key K
p, g, A = g^a mod p and B = g^b mod p
a and b
questions.explanation: The domain parameters and both half-keys travel openly; the private exponents and the derived K never leave the endpoints. An eavesdropper's task is to get K from the public values, which is the DH problem.
questions.concept: Public: p, g, A, B; secret: a, b, K.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which byte sequence begins a PDF file?
options: FF D8 FF
4D 5A ('MZ')
questions.explanation: PDFs start with %PDF. 4D 5A marks a Windows executable, FF D8 FF a JPEG and 89 50 4E 47 a PNG.
questions.concept: Magic numbers: PDF 25504446, EXE 4D5A, JPEG FFD8FF...FFD9, PNG 89504E47, ZIP 504B0304.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the purpose of the minimum hitting set (critical action set) computed from an attack graph?
options: To find the longest attack path
To find the attacker's identity
To list every vulnerability on every host
To find the smallest set of actions to block or patch that cuts every path from the start state to the goal
questions.explanation: Removing one action from each failing path removes all of them; the minimum set gives the cheapest defence. Listing every vulnerability is what isolated scanning already does.
questions.concept: Hitting set = minimal cut of all attack paths.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A user carries a laptop from home Wi-Fi to the office network. Which statement is correct?
options: Its IP address normally changes, while its NIC's MAC address normally stays the same
Both addresses stay the same because both are burned into the NIC
Its MAC address changes, while its IP address stays the same
Both addresses change because DHCP assigns MAC addresses
questions.explanation: IP addresses are logical and depend on the network the host joins; the MAC is the hardware address of the interface. DHCP assigns IP configuration, not MAC addresses, so the last option confuses the two layers.
questions.concept: MAC = local hardware identity (L2); IP = logical, location-dependent (L3).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Hosts 192.168.1.62/26 and 192.168.1.65/26 sit on the same switch with no router between them. Can they talk directly at Layer 3?
options: No: .62 is in 192.168.1.0/26 and .65 is in 192.168.1.64/26, so traffic must go through a router
Yes: consecutive addresses are always in the same subnet
Yes: they share the first three octets
No: .62 is the broadcast address of its subnet
questions.explanation: With /26, the boundaries fall at .0, .64, .128 and .192; .62 and .65 fall on opposite sides of .64. The broadcast of the first subnet is .63, not .62, so the last option is a near miss.
questions.concept: Same subnet means same result of IP AND mask.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A 3,000-byte PDF is attached using Base64 without line breaks. How many encoded characters result?
questions.explanation: Base64 maps every 3 input bytes to 4 output characters: 3,000 / 3 x 4 = 4,000. 3,000 assumes no overhead, which ignores that each character carries only 6 bits.
questions.concept: Base64 grows data by 4/3.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A server loop calls read(server_fd, buf, MAX) where server_fd is the listening socket, after new_socket = accept(server_fd, ...). Why does the transfer fail?
options: Data must be read from new_socket; the listening socket never carries user data
server_fd needs to be converted with htons() first
read() cannot be used on sockets; only recv() works
accept() must be called after read()
questions.explanation: The listening socket only queues connection requests; each accepted client gets its own descriptor for data. read() works on socket descriptors just like recv() with flags 0, so that is not the problem.
questions.concept: Use the descriptor returned by accept() for all data transfer.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Host B replies to Host A's ARP request. What is the destination MAC address of B's reply frame?
options: The default gateway's MAC address
A's MAC address (M_A)
B's own MAC address (M_B)
FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
questions.explanation: A's request carried its own MAC, so B can unicast the reply straight back to it. Broadcasting replies would waste bandwidth and expose mappings to every host for no reason.
questions.concept: ARP replies are unicast to the requester.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Every administrative action on a server is logged against an individual account. Which security objective does this mainly serve?
options: Traffic-flow confidentiality
Accountability, supporting non-repudiation, intrusion detection and forensics
Availability of the service
Confidentiality of stored files
questions.explanation: Tying each action to one entity allows tracing, after-action recovery and legal action. Logging does not keep files secret, so confidentiality is not its main aim.
questions.concept: Accountability = actions traceable to a responsible entity.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An etterfilter script replaces 'Welcome Guest' with 'AUTHORIZED USER' in HTTP responses. Which attack class is this, and what defeats it?
options: DoS; rate limiting defeats it
Replay; sequence numbers defeat it
Passive traffic analysis; traffic padding defeats it
Active modification in a man-in-the-middle position; end-to-end TLS defeats it
questions.explanation: The attacker alters content in transit, an integrity attack; with TLS the payload is encrypted and authenticated, so changes are detected. It is not passive, because data is changed.
questions.concept: Content rewriting in transit = modification; TLS prevents it.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: UDP has no SYN or FIN. How does a stateful firewall let DNS replies back in?
options: It converts DNS to TCP
It records the 4-tuple of the outbound query and accepts a matching reply within a short timeout
It allows all inbound UDP from port 53
It cannot; stateful filters only support TCP
questions.explanation: The firewall creates a pseudo-connection entry for the query and lets the matching reply through while the entry is fresh. Allowing all inbound UDP from port 53 is the stateless weakness attackers exploit.
questions.concept: Stateful UDP = 4-tuple entries with short timeouts.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does this Snort rule do? alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 23 (msg:"Telnet root"; flow:to_server,established; content:"root"; nocase; sid:1000005; rev:1;)
options: Raises an alert when an established Telnet session towards a home host carries 'root' in any letter case
Alerts on any packet from port 23 to any network
Logs only the first packet of each Telnet connection
Drops every Telnet packet containing 'root'
questions.explanation: The header limits it to TCP going to port 23 in HOME_NET, flow restricts it to established client-to-server traffic, and content/nocase match 'root'. The action is alert, so nothing is dropped.
questions.concept: Rule = action, header, then options that narrow the match.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Keyless transposition: write 'SECRETLINKNOW' row by row in rows of 4 (pad with Z), then read column by column. What is the ciphertext?
options: SECRETLINKNOWZZZ
ZOIRZNLCZKTEWNES
SCEERLTIKNNWOZZZ
SENWETKZCLNZRIOZ
questions.explanation: Rows: SECR / ETLI / NKNO / WZZZ. Reading down each column gives SENWETKZCLNZRIOZ. Reading the rows back gives the padded plaintext, which is no encryption at all.
questions.concept: Keyless columnar: write by rows, read by columns.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A ciphertext byte is 0x3A and the matching RC4 keystream byte is 0x5C. What is the plaintext byte?
options: 0x3A
questions.explanation: 0x3A XOR 0x5C = 0x66, which is ASCII 'f'. 0x96 is the arithmetic sum, not the XOR.
questions.concept: Decryption repeats the XOR.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: RSA with p = 19, q = 23, e = 5, so d = 317. A ciphertext c = 264 arrives. What is the plaintext?
questions.explanation: m = c^d mod n = 264^317 mod 437 = 42. Raising c to e (giving 120) encrypts again instead of decrypting.
questions.concept: m = c^d mod n.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: ESP uses AES-CBC (16-byte blocks). The payload is 45 bytes and the trailer adds Pad Length and Next Header (1 byte each). How many padding bytes are needed?
questions.explanation: 45 + 2 = 47 bytes; the next multiple of 16 is 48, so 1 padding byte(s). '3' pads the payload alone to 48 and forgets the 2 trailer bytes.
questions.concept: Pad so that payload + padding + 2 is a multiple of the block size.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A user deletes a file and empties the Recycle Bin on NTFS. Why can the file often be recovered?
options: Only the MFT record is marked as no longer in use; the data clusters remain until overwritten
NTFS keeps a hidden copy of every deleted file
The file is moved to a backup partition
Emptying the bin encrypts the file instead of deleting it
questions.explanation: Deletion changes the record's in-use flag and frees the clusters but does not wipe them. NTFS has no hidden copy; recovery works only while the space has not been reused.
questions.concept: Deletion != wiping.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Org1MSP calls TransferBatch on BATCH-1001 while its status is still CREATED. What does the chaincode do?
options: Rejects it, because transfer requires status QA_RELEASED
Sets the status to QA_RELEASED automatically
Deletes the batch
Transfers ownership and sets IN_TRANSIT
questions.explanation: TransferBatch checks that the caller owns the batch and that QA has released it. Automatically releasing would bypass the QA organisation's role, which is the point of the rule.
questions.concept: State machine: CREATED -> QA_RELEASED -> IN_TRANSIT -> RECEIVED.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An application sends a 70,000-byte JSON document in a single UDP datagram over IPv4 and it always fails. What is the best fix and reason?
options: Set the UDP Length field to 70,000
Rely on IP fragmentation, which allows datagrams up to 128 KB
Disable the UDP checksum to free space for the extra bytes
Use TCP or split the data at the application layer, because the IPv4 UDP payload limit is 65,507 bytes
questions.explanation: IPv4 total length is 16 bits (65,535), so 65,535 - 20 (IP) - 8 (UDP) = 65,507 bytes is the most a datagram can carry; larger data needs TCP or application chunking. The UDP Length field is also 16 bits, so it cannot hold 70,000.
questions.concept: Max IPv4 UDP payload = 65,535 - 20 - 8 = 65,507 bytes.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A vendor offers an 'unbreakable' affine cipher over letters whose algorithm is kept secret. Which critique is most accurate?
options: It is secure if the key is changed every year
It is secure because a secret algorithm cannot be analysed
It relies on secrecy of the algorithm (against Kerckhoffs), has only 312 keys, and leaks letter frequencies
It is weak only because the key is shorter than 56 bits
questions.explanation: Once the method leaks, 312 keys fall to brute force at once, and frequency analysis needs no brute force at all. Changing keys yearly does not fix either the tiny key space or the statistical leakage.
questions.concept: Judge a cipher assuming the attacker knows the algorithm.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An investigator wants a quick look at a suspect USB stick on a laptop before a meeting. Which approach best preserves evidential value?
options: Run an antivirus scan on the stick first to make it safe
Copy the visible files by drag and drop to the laptop
Open it in the file manager to browse quickly, then image it later
Attach it through a write-blocker, acquire a hashed .E01 image, verify the hash, and examine only the image
questions.explanation: Write-blocking and a verified image keep the original unaltered and give a hash to show the court. Browsing or scanning the original updates access times and may modify data; drag-and-drop also misses deleted and unallocated content.
questions.concept: Acquire first, verify, then analyse the copy.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A 2 GB transfer fails at 1.6 GB and resumes from the last saved marker instead of restarting. Which session-layer function made this possible?
options: Token management
Synchronisation and checkpointing
Framing
Dialogue control
questions.explanation: Checkpoints are inserted into long streams so recovery can restart from the last marker. Token management prevents two parties performing a critical action at once; it does not help with resumption.
questions.concept: Session layer: establish/terminate, dialogue control, checkpoints, tokens.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What are the default TCP ports for HTTP and HTTPS?
options: 21 and 22
questions.explanation: HTTP listens on TCP 80 by default and HTTPS on TCP 443. 8080 and 8443 are common alternates but not the defaults.
questions.concept: Well-known ports: HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP 21/20, SMTP 25, DNS 53.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: For IPv4, what is a socket address and how many bits does it occupy?
options: IP address alone: 32 bits
Two IP addresses: 64 bits
MAC address plus port: 48 + 16 = 64 bits
IP address plus port number: 32 + 16 = 48 bits
questions.explanation: A socket identifies one endpoint: the host's IP address and the process's port. A TCP connection is identified by the pair of sockets (the 4-tuple). MAC addresses play no part in socket identity.
questions.concept: Socket = IP + port; connection = client socket + server socket.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A booting client sends DHCP DISCOVER. Which source and destination IP addresses does it use?
options: Source 0.0.0.0, destination 255.255.255.255
Source 255.255.255.255, destination 0.0.0.0
Source 169.254.0.1, destination the server's IP
Source its last address, destination the gateway
questions.explanation: The client has no address yet and does not know the server, so it uses the unspecified source and the limited broadcast destination. It cannot address the server directly because it does not know the server's IP.
questions.concept: DISCOVER: 0.0.0.0 -> 255.255.255.255, MAC broadcast.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why is the emphasis for passive attacks on prevention rather than detection?
options: They alter nothing, so neither party sees any sign of them; encryption prevents the disclosure instead
They can be undone after the fact
They are always detected by intrusion detection systems
They only happen on wireless links
questions.explanation: A passive eavesdropper leaves traffic unchanged, so detection is nearly impossible; strong encryption and traffic padding make observation useless. IDS tools look for activity and cannot see a silent copy being taken.
questions.concept: Passive attacks: prevent with encryption and padding.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does TCP session hijacking differ from TCP session spoofing?
options: Hijacking uses UDP; spoofing uses TCP
Hijacking needs no sequence numbers; spoofing does
They are two names for the same attack
Hijacking takes over an existing connection; spoofing opens a new one while forging a trusted source address
questions.explanation: Hijacking injects packets with the right 4-tuple and predicted seq/ack into a live session; spoofing forges the SYN of a new connection, usually blind. Both depend on correct sequence numbers, so the third option is false.
questions.concept: Hijack = take over a live session; spoof = forge a new one.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which tcpdump options write raw packets to a file and read them back later?
options: -A to write; -X to read
-w file.pcap to write; -r file.pcap to read
-o to write; -i to read
-s to write; -c to read
questions.explanation: -w saves raw packets for offline analysis (for example in Wireshark) and -r replays a capture. -A and -X only change how payloads are printed.
questions.concept: Capture with -w, analyse with -r or Wireshark.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: When is a key k usable in the multiplicative cipher over Z_26, and how many such keys exist?
options: When gcd(k, 26) = 1; there are 12 keys
When k is prime; there are 9 keys
When k is odd; there are 13 keys
When k < 13; there are 12 keys
questions.explanation: k needs an inverse mod 26, which exists exactly when gcd(k, 26) = 1, giving phi(26) = 12 keys. 13 is odd but shares the factor 13 with 26, so 'all odd numbers' overcounts by one.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In RC4's PRGA, which value is output as the keystream byte?
options: T[i] XOR S[j]
S[(S[i] + S[j]) mod 256]
S[j] alone
S[i] + S[j]
questions.explanation: After i = i + 1, j = j + S[i] and the swap, the output index is t = (S[i] + S[j]) mod 256 and the byte is S[t]. S[i] + S[j] is the index, not the output.
questions.concept: Output k = S[t], t = S[i] + S[j] mod 256.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the standard countermeasure to man-in-the-middle attacks on DH and RSA key exchange?
options: Send the private exponent along with the public value
Use a smaller prime so the exchange runs faster
Authenticate public values with digital signatures and certificates from a trusted CA
Repeat the exchange twice
questions.explanation: Signed half-keys (authenticated DH, such as signed ECDHE in TLS) and certificate checks bind keys to identities. Repeating an unauthenticated exchange lets the attacker substitute keys twice.
questions.concept: Key exchange needs authentication.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What are the header and footer signatures of a JPEG file?
options: Header 50 4B 03 04, footer 50 4B 05 06
Header 89 50 4E 47, footer 49 45 4E 44
Header 25 50 44 46, footer 25 25 45 4F 46
Header FF D8 FF, footer FF D9
questions.explanation: JPEG starts with the SOI marker FF D8 and ends with EOI FF D9, which carving tools use to find file boundaries. 50 4B 03 04 is the ZIP family header.
questions.concept: JPEG: FF D8 FF ... FF D9.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does Hyperledger Fabric differ from a public blockchain such as Bitcoin?
options: It has no ledger, only a database
It is permissioned: every organisation, peer and user has a verified X.509 identity issued through an MSP
Anyone can join a channel without credentials
It uses proof-of-work mining by anonymous nodes
questions.explanation: Fabric is built for consortia with known members, using MSP identities and endorsement policies. Proof-of-work by anonymous miners describes Bitcoin.
questions.concept: Fabric = permissioned, identity-based.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An attacker forces a browser and server to negotiate TLS 1.0 instead of TLS 1.3, then exploits weaknesses in the old version. How should this be classified and fixed?
options: A Layer 2 replay attack; enable port security
A presentation-layer downgrade attack; disable deprecated protocol versions on servers and clients
A physical-layer wiretap; use shielded cabling
A transport-layer SYN flood; enable SYN cookies
questions.explanation: Downgrade attacks target the negotiation of cryptographic syntax, which the OSI model places at Layer 6; refusing old versions removes the fallback. SYN cookies address handshake-queue exhaustion, not cipher negotiation.
questions.concept: Downgrades are stopped by refusing weak versions, not by more bandwidth or filtering.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How many /28 subnets fit in one /24?
questions.explanation: Going from /24 to /28 borrows 4 bits, which gives 2^4 = 16 subnets of 16 addresses each. 14 is the number of usable hosts in each /28, not the number of subnets.
questions.concept: Subnets = 2^(new prefix - old prefix).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which MIME headers correctly describe a Base64-encoded PDF attachment?
options: MIME-Version: pdf and Content-Type: 7bit
Content-Type: base64 and Content-Transfer-Encoding: application/pdf
Content-Type: application/pdf and Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
Content-Encoding: smtp and Content-Type: text/plain
questions.explanation: Content-Type names the media type and Content-Transfer-Encoding names how it was converted for 7-bit transport. The second option swaps the two headers.
questions.concept: MIME headers: MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which set of calls does a simple UDP echo server use?
options: socket, bind, listen, accept
socket, listen, recvfrom, close
socket, connect, accept, send
socket, bind, recvfrom, sendto
questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless, so the server binds and then uses recvfrom/sendto, which carry the peer address on every datagram. listen() and accept() exist only for connection-oriented sockets.
questions.concept: UDP sockets skip listen/accept/connect (connect is optional).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which hosts should normally receive static DHCP bindings rather than pool leases?
options: Only hosts behind a relay agent
Every host, to avoid the overhead of leases
Infrastructure that must stay reachable at a fixed address, such as DNS servers, gateways and printers
Guest laptops that join for a few hours
questions.explanation: Fixed MAC-to-IP bindings suit services others depend on; transient clients should draw from the pool so addresses return when leases expire. Making every host static loses the flexibility that DHCP pools provide.
questions.concept: Static for infrastructure, dynamic for clients.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the four basic tasks in designing a security service in the network security model?
options: Generating the secret information used by it
Choosing the routing protocol for the backbone
Specifying a protocol for the parties to use the algorithm and secret
Designing the security transformation algorithm
questions.explanation: The four tasks are: design the algorithm, generate secret information, develop distribution and sharing methods, and specify the protocol. Routing protocol choice is network engineering, not security-service design.
questions.concept: Model: algorithm, secret, distribution, protocol.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: In blind TCP session spoofing against server B using trusted host A's address, why must the attacker first knock A offline?
options: Because B only accepts SYNs from offline hosts
Otherwise A would receive B's SYN-ACK and reset the connection with RST
Because A would encrypt the connection
Because A holds the ISN the attacker needs
questions.explanation: B's SYN-ACK goes to the real A, which never sent a SYN and would reply RST. The attacker must also predict B's ISN blind, since it never sees that SYN-ACK.
questions.concept: Session spoofing: silence the trusted host and guess the ISN.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Policy: only named staff may telnet out, and only after logging in; no inbound telnet. Which architecture meets it?
options: An application gateway that authenticates staff, plus a router filter allowing telnet only from the gateway's address
A DNS sinkhole for telnet hosts
A stateful filter tracking port 23 connections
A stateless filter allowing port 23 outbound
questions.explanation: Packet filters cannot see user identity; the gateway authenticates and relays, and the router ensures nobody bypasses it. A stateful filter knows connections, not people.
questions.concept: User-level policy needs a proxy.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which command correctly runs Snort 3 inline as an IPS between two interfaces?
options: sudo snort -T -i eth0 -A drop
sudo snort -c /etc/snort/snort.lua -i eth0 --mode inline
sudo snort -c /etc/snort/snort.lua -r capture.pcap -Q
sudo snort -c /etc/snort/snort.lua --daq afpacket -i eth0:eth1 -Q
questions.explanation: Inline mode in Snort 3 is -Q with an inline-capable DAQ and an interface pair. '--mode inline' is not a Snort 3 option, as the corrections note; -r reads a file offline, which cannot be inline.
questions.concept: Snort 3 inline: --daq afpacket -i a:b -Q.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An attacker knows every intercepted message begins 'Dear Customer' and has the matching ciphertexts, but cannot choose any inputs. Which attack model applies?
options: Ciphertext-only attack
Chosen-ciphertext attack
Known-plaintext attack
Chosen-plaintext attack
questions.explanation: The attacker holds plaintext-ciphertext pairs it did not choose, which is the known-plaintext model. Chosen-plaintext requires the ability to get arbitrary messages encrypted.
questions.concept: Fixed known pairs = KPA; oracle access = CPA/CCA.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Early Wi-Fi WEP fed RC4 a key made of a 24-bit IV concatenated with the network key, and used the keystream from the first byte. Which flaw does this create?
options: The IV makes each packet's key secret, so there is no flaw
The IV encrypts the key, doubling its length
Related keys with public IV bytes expose RC4's early-output biases, so enough packets reveal the network key
RC4 cannot accept keys longer than 24 bits
questions.explanation: The IV is sent in clear and shares the long-term key, and early RC4 bytes correlate with key bytes; collecting many packets recovers the key. Dropping initial output and deriving per-packet keys properly were later mitigations.
questions.concept: Public IV + related keys + early-byte bias = WEP break.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: For RSA with phi(n) = 120, which public exponent is NOT valid?
questions.explanation: e must satisfy gcd(e, phi(n)) = 1; gcd(9, 120) = 3, so 9 has no inverse and no d exists. 7, 11 and 13 share no factor with 120.
questions.concept: Valid e: 1 < e < phi(n) and gcd(e, phi(n)) = 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which IPsec combination both encrypts the data and hides the internal addresses of hosts behind two gateways?
options: ESP in transport mode
AH in transport mode
ESP in tunnel mode
AH in tunnel mode
questions.explanation: Tunnel mode puts the inner header inside the protected payload and ESP encrypts it, so only gateway addresses are visible. AH in tunnel mode hides nothing, because AH does not encrypt.
questions.concept: Confidentiality + hidden topology = ESP tunnel.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A UserAssist registry value name reads 'abgrcnq.rkr'. What program does it record?
options: mspaint.exe
notepad.exe
nopetad.exe
abgrcnq.rkr
questions.explanation: UserAssist names are ROT13-encoded; shifting each letter 13 places turns 'abgrcnq.rkr' back into 'notepad.exe'. ROT13 is its own inverse and leaves the dot unchanged.
questions.concept: UserAssist uses ROT13 obfuscation.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A user with the Org1 identity invokes ReleaseBatch. What happens?
options: Rejected: only Org2MSP (the QA organisation) may release a batch
Accepted, but only if quantity > 0
Accepted, because Org1 owns the batch
Queued until Org2 approves
questions.explanation: The chaincode checks the caller's MSP ID and allows release only by Org2MSP, separating manufacturing from QA. Ownership does not grant release rights.
questions.concept: Authorisation by MSP identity inside chaincode.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Hosts on subnets 2-4 cannot obtain addresses after a re-design; the single DHCP server sits on subnet 1. Which fix is best?
options: Replace DHCP with a static BOOTP table on the same server
Configure a DHCP relay agent (helper address) on each remote subnet's router interface pointing to the server
Increase the lease time on the existing server
Let routers forward 255.255.255.255 between all subnets
questions.explanation: Relays carry DISCOVER/REQUEST across routers as unicast and keep broadcasts contained. Forwarding limited broadcasts everywhere risks broadcast storms and still does not scale; longer leases do nothing for hosts that never reach the server.
questions.concept: Centralised DHCP across subnets requires relay agents.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which change turns a repeating-key XOR scheme into one with perfect secrecy?
options: Keep the XOR algorithm secret
Use a 256-bit key and repeat it across the message
Encrypt the message twice with the same key
Use a truly random key as long as each message, and never use any key twice
questions.explanation: Perfect secrecy needs fresh, uniformly random key material for every bit; a repeated key leaks patterns however long it is. XORing twice with the same key cancels out and returns the plaintext.
questions.concept: Perfect secrecy is about key length, randomness and single use.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which body of evidence best supports a claim in court that a departing employee copied a specific design file to a USB stick?
options: The USBSTOR serial and connection times, matching file-system and LNK timestamps, the hash of the carved file matching the original, and documented chain of custody
The fact that the USB stick is now empty
The employee's browser history alone
A signature mismatch on an unrelated file
questions.explanation: Device identity, time correlation, a content hash match and custody records together tie person, device, time and file. An empty stick proves nothing without carving and correlation.
questions.concept: Correlate device, time, content and custody.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which control most directly mitigates MAC flooding on an access switch?
options: A web application firewall
DNSSEC validation
TCP SYN cookies
Port security limiting the number of MAC addresses learned per port
questions.explanation: MAC flooding overfills the switch's CAM table; capping learned addresses per port stops one port from injecting thousands of bogus MACs. SYN cookies protect TCP connection queues on servers and have no effect on a switch's CAM table.
questions.concept: MAC flooding -> port security; ARP spoofing -> DAI; rogue DHCP -> DHCP snooping.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which HTTP method returns only the status line and headers, not the body?
options: HEAD
GET
TRACE
OPTIONS
questions.explanation: HEAD behaves like GET but the server omits the body, which is useful for checking size or freshness. OPTIONS lists the methods a resource supports; it is not a body-less GET.
questions.concept: HEAD = GET without the body.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which port range is used for dynamic (ephemeral) client ports?
questions.explanation: Well-known ports are 0-1,023, registered ports 1,024-49,151 and dynamic/private ports 49,152-65,535. Some operating systems use their own ephemeral ranges, but the IANA definition is the last block.
questions.concept: Ports: well-known / registered / dynamic.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the correct order of the DHCP exchange?
options: OFFER, DISCOVER, ACK, REQUEST
DISCOVER, REQUEST, OFFER, ACK
DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK
REQUEST, OFFER, DISCOVER, ACK
questions.explanation: The client discovers servers, receives offers, requests one offered address, and the server acknowledges the lease (DORA). Requesting before any offer arrives would leave the client nothing to request.
questions.concept: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does data-origin authentication NOT protect against?
options: Messages claiming a false origin
Connectionless messages such as e-mail
Forgery of the sender's identity
Duplication (replay) or modification of data units
questions.explanation: Data-origin authentication confirms where a data unit came from but does not stop it being replayed or altered; integrity and anti-replay services handle those. It is designed for connectionless traffic such as e-mail, so that option describes where it is used.
questions.concept: Origin authentication is not integrity or anti-replay.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is pharming?
options: Overloading a DNS server with queries
Maliciously altering hostname-to-IP mappings so users reach an attacker's server
Guessing passwords for DNS administrator accounts
Sending bulk e-mail with malicious links
questions.explanation: Pharming corrupts name resolution (a compromised server or spoofed replies), often paired with a phishing replica site. Bulk e-mail with links is phishing alone, which does not touch DNS.
questions.concept: Pharming = DNS mapping corruption; phishing = deceptive replica.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does an nmap SYN scan (-sS) work?
options: It sends SYN, reads SYN-ACK (open) or RST (closed), and resets instead of completing the handshake
It sends only ACK packets to map firewall rules
It sends UDP datagrams to every port
It completes the full three-way handshake for every port
questions.explanation: The half-open scan never finishes the connection, which makes it fast and quieter; it needs root to craft raw packets. The full handshake is -sT, the connect scan.
questions.concept: -sS half-open (root); -sT full connect (non-root).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the key-space size of the affine cipher over Z_26?
questions.explanation: k1 has 12 valid choices and k2 has 26: 12 x 26 = 312. 676 = 26 x 26 wrongly allows k1 values without inverses.
questions.concept: Affine keys = phi(26) x 26 = 312.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does RC4 encrypt and decrypt?
options: Ciphertext = plaintext + keystream mod 256; decryption uses a different key
Ciphertext = plaintext XOR keystream; decryption XORs the same keystream again
Decryption runs the PRGA backwards
RC4 permutes plaintext bytes using S
questions.explanation: Like every additive stream cipher, the same keystream XORed twice cancels out. RC4 does not permute the plaintext; S is internal state.
questions.concept: Stream encryption and decryption are the same XOR.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which IP protocol numbers identify AH and ESP?
options: AH = 50, ESP = 51
AH = 4, ESP = 41
AH = 51, ESP = 50
AH = 6, ESP = 17
questions.explanation: AH is protocol 51 and ESP is 50. 6 and 17 are TCP and UDP; 4 and 41 are IPv4-in-IP and IPv6-in-IP.
questions.concept: AH 51, ESP 50.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does a write-blocker do during acquisition?
options: Speeds up imaging by caching writes
Lets the examiner read the suspect media while preventing any write to it
Deletes temporary files from the suspect drive
Encrypts the evidence drive
questions.explanation: Even mounting a drive normally can alter timestamps, which damages evidential value; a hardware or software write-blocker passes reads and blocks writes. Deleting anything from evidence is exactly what must never happen.
questions.concept: Golden rule: never alter original evidence.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does Fabric's ordering service do?
options: Orders endorsed transactions into blocks and distributes them; it does not execute chaincode
Executes chaincode and signs endorsements
Issues X.509 identities
Stores the world state in CouchDB
questions.explanation: Ordering is separated from execution: peers simulate and endorse, the orderer sequences, and peers validate and commit. Issuing identities is the certificate authority's or MSP's role.
questions.concept: Orderer orders; peers execute and validate.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A frame arrives at R1 with a failed FCS check. What happens next?
options: R1 corrects the flipped bits using the CRC and forwards the frame
R1 forwards the frame and lets the destination decide
R1 discards the frame; recovery, if any, is left to higher layers such as TCP retransmission
R1 sends an ICMP Parameter Problem message to the next hop
questions.explanation: CRC in the FCS detects errors but cannot locate or correct them, so the damaged frame is dropped at that hop. Claiming CRC corrects errors confuses error detection with error-correcting codes.
questions.concept: FCS/CRC = hop-by-hop error detection; reliability comes from upper layers.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is the last usable host address in 200.10.1.64/27?
questions.explanation: A /27 has 32 addresses: .64-.95. The broadcast is 200.10.1.95, so the last host is 200.10.1.94. .95 is the broadcast and cannot be assigned to a host.
questions.concept: Last host = broadcast - 1; first host = network + 1.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A user resolves www.news.example twice within the record's TTL. What normally happens on the second lookup?
options: The client queries the authoritative server directly
The resolver repeats the full root-TLD-authoritative walk
The root server answers from its own cache
The local resolver answers from its cache without contacting the root, TLD or authoritative servers
questions.explanation: Resolvers cache answers for the TTL, which removes DNS overhead for repeat lookups. Root servers do not hold host records, so they cannot answer from cache.
questions.concept: Caching with TTL avoids repeated hierarchical lookups.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Data 1101011 is protected with generator 1101 (degree 3). What CRC remainder is appended?
questions.explanation: Append three zeros (1101011000) and divide modulo 2 by 1101 using XOR; the remainder is 010, so the codeword is 1101011010. Using ordinary subtraction with borrows instead of XOR gives a wrong remainder.
questions.concept: CRC: append (degree) zeros, divide modulo 2, append the remainder.
questions.source: Scenario type: Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, ch. 10

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Router R3 discards a datagram sent from S to R. What are the source and destination addresses of the ICMP error?
options: Source R3, destination S
Source R, destination S
Source S, destination R
Source R3, destination R
questions.explanation: The router that drops the datagram originates the ICMP message and addresses it to the datagram's original source. Sending it to R would inform the wrong party, since R never received the datagram.
questions.concept: icmp(R3, S): from the discarding node to the source.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An insider with a valid account edits payroll records in a way the policy forbids. Which property is breached?
options: Integrity (data changed in an unauthorised manner)
Non-repudiation
Availability
Confidentiality
questions.explanation: Integrity means data changes only in specified, authorised ways; a valid login does not authorise forbidden edits. Nothing was disclosed or made unavailable.
questions.concept: Authorised access is not the same as authorised change.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: After a starvation flood stops, how does a 1-hour lease time compare with a 24-hour lease?
options: Exhaustion speed is the same, but spoofed leases expire and the pool recovers much sooner with 1 hour
Lease time affects neither exhaustion nor recovery
The pool is exhausted 24 times more slowly with 1-hour leases
Shorter leases make the attack impossible
questions.explanation: Exhaustion depends on free addresses and request rate, not lease length; lease length governs how long stolen addresses stay unavailable. Shorter leases do not stop a flood that keeps going.
questions.concept: Lease time sets the length of the outage, not how fast the pool runs out.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: The authoritative server for univ-a.example is compromised. Its replies add glue saying bank.example is at the attacker's address. Which resolver behaviour prevents poisoning?
options: Using TCP for the query
Caching glue only for the TTL given
Querying the root server first
Rejecting glue for names outside the queried zone (bailiwick checking)
questions.explanation: The univ-a.example server has no authority over bank.example, so that glue must be discarded. Honouring the TTL still caches the poison for that whole period.
questions.concept: Out-of-bailiwick glue must not be cached.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which command captures DNS traffic on eth0 with numeric output only?
options: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'udp port 67'
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A 'tcp port 80'
sudo tcpdump -r eth0 'udp port 53'
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -nn 'udp port 53'
questions.explanation: DNS uses UDP 53, -i selects the interface and -nn disables name lookups. -r reads a saved file rather than a live interface, and port 67 is DHCP.
questions.concept: Interface with -i, filter at the end, -nn for numbers.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Two one-byte messages were encrypted with the same pad byte, giving ciphertexts 0x5A and 0x3C. What does an eavesdropper learn without the key?
options: The pad byte = 0x96
Nothing, because the pad is random
m1 = 0x5A and m2 = 0x3C
m1 XOR m2 = 0x66
questions.explanation: c1 XOR c2 = (m1 XOR k) XOR (m2 XOR k) = m1 XOR m2 = 0x5A XOR 0x3C = 0x66, which leaks the relationship between the plaintexts. 0x96 = 0x5A + 0x3C uses addition instead of XOR, and the pad does not cancel to reveal itself.
questions.concept: Pad reuse: c1 XOR c2 = m1 XOR m2.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: RC4's second output byte equals 0 with probability about 2/256 instead of 1/256. What can an attacker do with this?
options: Distinguish RC4 output from random and, over many encryptions of the same plaintext, infer the second plaintext byte
Recover the full key from one ciphertext
Decrypt AES traffic on the same link
Nothing, because 2/256 is negligible
questions.explanation: Collecting many ciphertexts of the same plaintext shows which second byte appears most often; since the keystream byte is often 0, that value is likely the plaintext byte. A single ciphertext does not reveal the key from this bias alone.
questions.concept: Small biases become attacks with many samples.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A client accepts whatever RSA public key arrives over the socket. An attacker intercepts the server's key and forwards its own. What happens to the client's message?
options: The server detects the swap because the ciphertext is too long
The message is lost, because two public keys conflict
It is encrypted with the attacker's key; the attacker decrypts, reads or alters it, and re-encrypts it with the server's real key
It cannot be read, because the attacker lacks the server's private key
questions.explanation: Without certificate checks, the client cannot tell the attacker's key from the server's, so the attacker relays transparently. The server's private key is not needed, because the client never used the server's public key.
questions.concept: Unauthenticated public keys enable relay MitM.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Two hosts use ESP in transport mode. What can an eavesdropper still see?
options: The TCP ports and payload
Nothing; transport mode encrypts the IP header
The original IP header (source and destination), plus the ESP SPI and sequence number
Only the outer gateway addresses
questions.explanation: Transport mode keeps the original IP header in clear; ESP encrypts the TCP/UDP header and data. Gateway-only addresses would mean tunnel mode.
questions.concept: Transport ESP exposes who talks to whom, not what they say.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: During an EnCase case, where should the examiner save exported files and reports?
options: On the suspect drive, next to the originals
On the processing cache volume
On a separate read/write output volume, never on the evidence drive
In the same folder as the .E01 images
questions.explanation: Separating evidence (read-only), processing cache and outputs keeps evidence untouched and organised. Writing to the suspect drive alters evidence, which breaks the golden rule.
questions.concept: Evidence, cache and outputs on separate volumes.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An invoke returns a successful endorsement, but a later query still shows the old state. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Queries always lag by one block
The transaction was not committed, for example failing validation (endorsement policy or MVCC read-set conflict)
Endorsement always equals commit, so the query is wrong
The orderer executed a different version of the chaincode
questions.explanation: Endorsement is only simulation; validation at commit can still invalidate the transaction, which is why the lab says to query afterwards. The orderer does not execute chaincode at all.
questions.concept: Endorsed is not the same as committed.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A security team proposes blocking all ICMP at the perimeter. Which policy is best justified?
options: Block only inbound Echo Reply and allow Source Quench to slow attackers
Permit essential ICMP errors such as Destination Unreachable (including fragmentation-needed), rate-limit Echo, and drop outbound Time Exceeded to hinder mapping
Allow all ICMP, because it never carries data
Block all ICMP; TCP and UDP report their own errors, so nothing breaks
questions.explanation: Blanket blocking breaks path-MTU discovery and diagnostics, while allowing everything invites floods and mapping; selective rules keep function and reduce exposure. Source Quench is deprecated and no defence, and transport protocols rely on ICMP signals such as fragmentation-needed.
questions.concept: Filter ICMP by type, not all-or-nothing.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Alice and Bob try the three-pass 'two padlocks' protocol using XOR as the lock: Alice sends M^A, Bob returns M^A^B, Alice sends M^B. Is it safe against an eavesdropper who sees all three messages?
options: No: XORing the three messages gives (M^A) ^ (M^A^B) ^ (M^B) = M, so the eavesdropper recovers M
Yes: without A or B the messages are random
No, but only because XOR cannot be undone
Yes, as long as A and B are each 128 bits
questions.explanation: XOR locks commute, which the protocol needs, but they also cancel when combined, so the three transcripts together reveal M. The protocol needs a commutative operation that does not leak in this way, such as modular exponentiation.
questions.concept: Commutative locks must not cancel out in the transcript.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An attack graph has three paths: {A, B, D}, {A, C, D} and {E, C, F}. Patch costs are A = 5, B = 2, C = 1, D = 3, E = 4, F = 6. Which choice is the cheapest set that cuts every path?
options: Patch A and C (cost 6)
Patch B and C (cost 3)
Patch C and D (cost 4)
Patch C only (cost 1)
questions.explanation: No single action lies on all three paths: C misses {A, B, D}. Among pairs that cut all three paths, {B, C} costs 2 + 1 = 3, less than {C, D} = 4 or {A, C} = 6.
questions.concept: Minimum-cost hitting set: every path must lose at least one action.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How long is an IPv4 address?
options: 32 bits (four octets)
128 bits (sixteen octets)
64 bits (eight octets)
48 bits (six octets)
questions.explanation: IPv4 uses 32 bits, written as four dotted-decimal octets, giving 2^32 (about 4.29 billion) addresses. 48 bits is the length of a MAC address, a frequent mix-up.
questions.concept: IPv4 = 32 bits; MAC = 48 bits; IPv6 = 128 bits.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How do SMTP and POP3/IMAP divide the work of e-mail delivery?
options: POP3 pushes mail between servers; SMTP pulls it to the reader
SMTP pushes mail from client to server and between servers; POP3/IMAP pull it from the mailbox to the reader
IMAP relays mail between servers; SMTP is only for attachments
SMTP handles both sending and mailbox retrieval
questions.explanation: SMTP is a push protocol used by mail transfer agents; the recipient's access agent uses POP3 or IMAP to pull stored messages. SMTP has no mailbox-retrieval role, which rules out the third option.
questions.concept: SMTP = push (MTA); POP3/IMAP = pull (MAA).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which server-side socket call dequeues a pending connection and returns a new descriptor for data transfer?
options: bind()
connect()
accept()
listen()
questions.explanation: accept() blocks until a client is queued, then returns a new socket for that client while the listening socket keeps waiting for others. listen() only marks the socket passive and sets the queue size.
questions.concept: Listening socket waits; accept() creates a per-client data socket.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which ICMP messages does ping use?
options: Echo Request and Echo Reply
Time Exceeded and Destination Unreachable
Source Quench and Redirect
Parameter Problem and Echo Reply
questions.explanation: ping sends Echo Requests and waits for Echo Replies to confirm network-layer reachability. Time Exceeded is what traceroute relies on.
questions.concept: ping = echo; traceroute = TTL + Time Exceeded.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which X.800 mechanism is specifically aimed at defeating traffic analysis?
options: Traffic padding
Digital signature
Access control
Notarisation
questions.explanation: Padding inserts dummy traffic or fills messages to uniform size so patterns and volumes reveal nothing. Notarisation uses a trusted third party for assurance and does not hide patterns.
questions.concept: Traffic-flow confidentiality: encipherment, padding, routing control.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A resolver accepts a DNS reply only if which values match its outstanding query?
options: The TTL and the record type only
The MAC address of the authoritative server
Source/destination IP addresses, UDP ports and the 16-bit transaction ID
The TCP sequence number
questions.explanation: Matching addresses, ports and ID is all basic DNS checks, which is why guessing them enables spoofing. DNS queries normally use UDP, so there is no TCP sequence number to match.
questions.concept: Spoofed DNS reply must match IPs, ports and TXID.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which nmap option performs host discovery without a port scan?
options: -A
-sV
-sn
-Pn
questions.explanation: -sn (ping scan) lists live hosts only. -Pn does the opposite: it skips discovery and treats every host as up.
questions.concept: -sn = discovery only; -Pn = skip discovery.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does a transposition cipher differ from a substitution cipher?
options: It replaces each symbol with a different one
It needs two keys instead of one
It always works on bits rather than letters
It keeps the original symbols but changes their positions
questions.explanation: Transposition only reorders, so letter frequencies are unchanged; substitution replaces symbols. Key count is a separate dimension from the type of operation.
questions.concept: Substitution replaces; transposition reorders.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why has RC4 been prohibited in modern TLS?
options: Its key length is fixed at 40 bits
It is too slow in software
It cannot encrypt bytes, only bits
Statistical biases in its keystream, such as the second-byte bias, allow practical plaintext recovery
questions.explanation: Biases (for example, the second output byte is 0 with probability about 2/256) accumulate over many sessions and were exploited against TLS and WEP. RC4 is fast and supports long keys, so neither is the reason.
questions.concept: RC4 biases led to its removal from TLS.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which service does the Authentication Header (AH) NOT provide?
options: Anti-replay protection
Data-origin authentication
Confidentiality (encryption)
Connectionless integrity
questions.explanation: AH authenticates and protects against replay, but the payload travels in clear. Encryption is ESP's addition.
questions.concept: AH: integrity, origin, anti-replay; no encryption.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: How does file carving recover deleted files?
options: It restores files from the operating system's recycle bin
It decrypts the file system journal
It scans raw (often unallocated) sectors for known headers and footers and extracts the bytes between them
It asks the file system table where the deleted file was
