questions.explanation: Deletion usually just marks the directory entry free, so the data remains until overwritten; carving ignores file-system metadata and works on content signatures. Using the file-system table is ordinary recovery, which fails once the entry is gone.
questions.concept: Carving = signature-based recovery from raw data.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What is Fabric's transaction flow?
options: Validate, mine, broadcast
Commit, then endorse
Execute (endorse), order, validate and commit
Order, execute, mine
questions.explanation: Clients get endorsements from simulated execution, the orderer builds blocks, and every peer validates signatures and MVCC versions before committing. Mining is not part of Fabric.
questions.concept: Execute-order-validate.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Which Layer 3 control helps drop packets with forged source addresses by checking that the return path uses the arrival interface?
options: Session timeout
Dynamic ARP Inspection
Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF)
HttpOnly cookies
questions.explanation: uRPF looks up the packet's source address and drops it if the route back would not use the interface it came in on, which catches many spoofed sources. Dynamic ARP Inspection validates ARP at Layer 2 and does not check IP source routes.
questions.concept: IP spoofing mitigation: uRPF and ingress filtering.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What prefix length does 255.255.255.240 represent, and how many usable hosts does it give?
options: /27 with 30 usable hosts
/29 with 6 usable hosts
/28 with 14 usable hosts
/28 with 16 usable hosts
questions.explanation: 240 = 11110000, so the mask has 24 + 4 = 28 one-bits and 4 host bits: 16 addresses, 14 usable. 16 hosts forgets the two reserved addresses.
questions.concept: Count mask 1-bits for the prefix; host bits = 32 - prefix.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A firewall allows TCP 21 to an FTP server, but directory listings and downloads fail. What best explains this?
options: FTP shares the HTTP connection on port 80
FTP needs UDP 21 as well
The control channel closes after login
File data uses a separate data connection that the rule does not permit
questions.explanation: FTP is out-of-band: commands work on port 21, but listings and files flow over separate data connections (port 20 in active mode, or a dynamic port). The control channel stays open for the whole session, so its closing is not the cause.
questions.concept: Out-of-band protocols need rules for every channel.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: With generator 1011, the receiver gets codeword 1010011101. The remainder after modulo-2 division is 101. What should it conclude?
options: No error, because the leading bit is 1
An error is detected because the remainder is non-zero
The error is in the last three bits and can be fixed in place
The generator must have changed in transit
questions.explanation: A valid codeword divides exactly (remainder 000); any non-zero remainder such as 101 flags corruption, and ARQ would request retransmission. A plain CRC does not locate the flipped bit, so correcting it in place is not possible.
questions.concept: Remainder 0 = accept; non-zero = error detected.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Host 192.168.1.20/24 sends to 8.8.4.4. Whose MAC address does it resolve with ARP?
options: The broadcast MAC FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
The MAC of 8.8.4.4
Its default gateway's MAC address
No MAC is needed for off-subnet traffic
questions.explanation: ARP only works on the local link; for an off-subnet destination the frame goes to the gateway, so the host resolves the gateway's IP. The remote server's MAC is never visible across routers.
questions.concept: Off-subnet destination: ARP for the next hop (gateway), not the final host.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: According to the X.800 service-mechanism table, which mechanism is NOT used for peer-entity authentication?
options: Encipherment
Authentication exchange
Traffic padding
Digital signature
questions.explanation: Peer-entity authentication uses encipherment, digital signatures and authentication exchange. Traffic padding serves traffic-flow confidentiality.
questions.concept: Map each service to its mechanisms.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An attacker on a LAN with encrypted Wi-Fi payloads records source/destination MACs, frame sizes and timing to map hosts. How does X.800 classify this?
options: Modification of messages, an active attack
Traffic analysis, a passive attack
Masquerade, an active attack
Denial of service, an active attack
questions.explanation: Nothing is changed; the attacker learns from visible Layer 2 headers and patterns. Masquerade would need the attacker to pose as another station, for example through MAC spoofing.
questions.concept: Observing headers and patterns = traffic analysis.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A first-match ACL reads: (1) allow TCP any -> 10.0.0.5:80; (2) deny TCP any -> any:80; (3) allow any -> any. What happens to a TCP packet to 10.0.0.7:80?
options: Allowed by rule 3
Denied because no rule matches
Denied by rule 2
Allowed by rule 1
questions.explanation: Rule 1 matches only 10.0.0.5, so the packet falls to rule 2, which matches port 80 to any host and denies. Rule 3 is never reached for this packet, because evaluation stops at the first match.
questions.concept: Packet filters apply the first matching rule.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: What does 'cat subs.txt | httprobe -p http:8080 --prefer-https' produce for a host that serves both HTTP and HTTPS on 443/80?
options: A full port scan of each host
Both http:// and https:// URLs for 80 and 443, but nothing for 8080
Only the https:// URL for that host, plus any responsive http://host:8080
Nothing, because -p disables default ports
questions.explanation: --prefer-https skips the HTTP probe when HTTPS answers, and -p adds the custom port. Default ports are dropped only with -s, not with -p.
questions.concept: httprobe: -p adds ports, -s skips defaults, --prefer-https avoids duplicates.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A monoalphabetic substitution with a random 26-letter table has about 2^88 keys. Why is it still broken quickly?
options: Letter frequencies survive encryption, so frequency analysis recovers the mapping without searching keys
It is a transposition cipher, so letters are unchanged
2^88 keys can be brute-forced in minutes
The table must be public under Kerckhoffs' principle
questions.explanation: Each plaintext letter always maps to the same ciphertext letter, so the most common ciphertext letters reveal E, T, A and so on. 2^88 is far beyond practical brute force; the weakness is statistical.
questions.concept: Large key space is necessary, not sufficient.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A chat app seeds RC4 with the same shared secret for every message, restarting the keystream each time. What is the consequence?
options: Every message uses the same keystream, so XORing two ciphertexts yields the XOR of their plaintexts
Nothing, because RC4's state is reshuffled by each message
The messages become impossible to decrypt
Only the first message is exposed
questions.explanation: Restarting RC4 with the same key repeats the keystream exactly, which is pad reuse. RC4's state depends only on the key, not on previous messages, after a restart.
questions.concept: Never reuse a stream-cipher key and nonce pair.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A voting app sends textbook RSA encryptions of 'yes' or 'no'. Why can an eavesdropper learn each vote?
options: The public key reveals the private key for short messages
RSA can only encrypt numbers, not words
The ciphertext is always the same length as the plaintext
RSA without padding is deterministic, so encrypting both candidate answers with the public key and comparing reveals the vote
questions.explanation: With a tiny message space the attacker simply tries each possibility; randomised padding (OAEP) makes each encryption different. Public keys do not reveal private keys; the weakness is determinism.
questions.concept: Deterministic encryption fails for small message spaces.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A branch gateway's policy: traffic to head office 10.1.0.0/16 must be protected; traffic to the local printer stays in clear; inbound Telnet from the Internet is never allowed. Which SPD actions match?
options: Bypass; apply IPsec; discard
Apply IPsec; bypass; discard
Discard; bypass; apply IPsec
Apply IPsec; discard; bypass
questions.explanation: Head-office traffic uses an SA (apply), printer traffic passes in clear (bypass), and forbidden Telnet is dropped (discard). Bypassing head-office traffic would send it unprotected across the Internet.
questions.concept: SPD selectors map traffic classes to actions.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: An image uses blocks of 64 sectors of 512 bytes. How many blocks does a 16 GiB drive produce?
questions.explanation: Block size = 64 x 512 = 32,768 bytes (32 KiB); 16 GiB / 32 KiB = 524,288 blocks. 33,554,432 is the number of sectors, not blocks.
questions.concept: Blocks = capacity / (sectors per block x sector size).

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: Why does ReadBatch, marked as an EVALUATE transaction, not create a block?
options: It is rejected by the orderer
It needs both organisations to endorse it first
Reads are written to a separate ledger
It is a query evaluated on one peer's world state and is not submitted for ordering
questions.explanation: Evaluate transactions read state without changing it, so there is nothing to order or commit. Endorsement by both organisations matters only for submitted transactions.
questions.concept: Evaluate = read-only query; submit = endorse, order, commit.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A hospital's e-prescription system must ensure a doctor's order is not altered and cannot later be disowned. Which design best meets this?
options: Use routing control to send orders only over private lines
Doctors sign orders with private keys; the pharmacy verifies signatures; tamper-evident audit logs record each action
Encrypt orders with one key shared by all doctors and pharmacists
Add traffic padding to the link between clinic and pharmacy
questions.explanation: Signatures give integrity and non-repudiation of origin, and audit logs add accountability. A shared key can keep orders secret but cannot show which person wrote an order, since every key holder could have.
questions.concept: Integrity + non-repudiation -> digital signatures + audit.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: A designer proposes encrypting sensor readings with the output of a single 16-bit LFSR whose seed is the secret key. Which assessment is correct?
options: Secure, provided the taps are kept secret as well
Insecure only because 16-bit keys are too short to brute force
Secure, because the period can reach 65,535 bits
Insecure: about 32 known keystream bits let an attacker solve for the taps and state, so a guessable reading format exposes everything
questions.explanation: Linear complexity, not period, governs security: 2L = 32 bits of keystream reveal the register even if the taps are unknown. Brute force of 2^16 is also easy, but the algebraic attack applies even to much longer LFSRs.
questions.concept: Never use a lone LFSR as a cipher.

questions.subject: Networking
questions.stem: You must add RecallBatch to the pharma chaincode. Which rule design keeps the ledger's guarantees?
options: Org1 may call it and reset the status to CREATED so the batch can be shipped again
Only Org2MSP (QA) may call it, from QA_RELEASED, IN_TRANSIT or RECEIVED; it sets status RECALLED and later transfers reject RECALLED batches
Any organisation may call it from any state, and it deletes the batch record
The ordering service calls it automatically when a block is full
questions.explanation: Recall is a QA decision, must apply to released stock, and should be recorded as a new state rather than erasing history. Deleting the record destroys the audit trail, and resetting to CREATED lets recalled stock re-enter the supply chain.
questions.concept: Extend state machines with explicit, authorised, auditable transitions.
